Abstract:
Screw conveyors are intended for the short-distance transportation of bulk materials in food, agricultural, energy, or lime industry plants. They are also used when other processes, such as mixing, heating, cooling, drying, moistening, or precise proportioning, are required. A screw conveyor can be used for transportation in three planes: vertical, horizontal, or at a certain inclination angle. Simple construction and working principle, together with an easy adjustment of their efficiency through the change of the shaft’s rotational speed, are the key advantages of the screw conveyors. Currently, screw conveyors can be equipped with screw flights of diverse shapes. Depending on the application, the screws may have varying pitches, conical internal and external diameters through the whole length, and the flights may be irregular in shape. In so-called reversible conveyors, used for bi-directional transportation of material, we can even find flights of opposite twist directions mounted on one shaft. Such untypical constructions of screws are possible with advanced flight production technologies, such as forming in hydraulic presses without preheating the prefabricated parts. Producing any shapes and sizes of the screw flights is not a technological problem. What is challenging for the engineers is the designing process of the screw conveyors. Their construction and exploitation parameters must meet the defined requirements concerning the mass efficiency, filling rate of the trough, or providing the necessary power to the drive. The behavior of bulk materials during transportation by a screw conveyor is very complicated. It depends on many factors, such as the type and shape of the screw flights, the rotational speed of the shaft, the way of proportioning of the material, or the physical properties of the material. Theoretical methods for designing the screw conveyors do not consider all the factors mentioned above or oversimplify them. In the case of typical bulk materials of uniform granulation and standard constructions of the screws (constant pitch, constant internal and external diameters) and fed by one source, e.g., a hopper, theoretical methods allow reasonable estimation of the exploitation parameters of the screw conveyors. In the case of materials of specific properties (cohesive or strongly aerated materials) or for unusual shapes of screws or multiple feeding points, these methods do not provide reliable results of efficiency and power [16]. For this reason, the external diameters of the screws and power demands are very often chosen to be safely larger. Such an approach is unfavorable because of the excessive use of materials, ineffective use of the drive unit, and high exploitation costs. On the other hand, the difficulties in making decisions on the construction of screw conveyors are caused The paper describes the problem of designing screw conveyors in terms of determining their exploitation characteristics. Based on the actual values of mass efficiency and power demand obtained in a laboratory experiment, the theoretical design methods and the numerical discrete element method model results were verified. The obtained results have shown that the currently used theoretical methods underestimate the mass efficiency and power demand compared to experiments when typical values of filling rate coefficient and progress resistance coefficient are used. It was also shown that the results of DEM simulations are in good agreement with the experiments in terms of mass efficiency and power demand. Based on the exploitation characteristics determined in DEM simulations for different constructions of the screw and different rotational speeds, multi-objective optimization of the exploitation parameters of the screw was performed in order to minimize the power demand of a screw conveyor and simultaneously maximize its mass efficiency. The optimization results showed that it is possible to find such construction and the rotational speed that will maximize the mass efficiency of the conveyor and keep the power demand low, reducing the exploitation costs of the device. Abstract:
Vertical stirred mills have been widely applied in the minerals industry, due to its greater efficiency in comparison with conventional tumbling mills. In this context, the agitator liner wear plays an important role in maintenance planning and operational costs. In this paper, we use the discrete element method (DEM) wear simulation to evaluate the screw liner wear. Three different mill rotational velocities are evaluated in the simulation, according to different scale-up procedures. The wear profile, wear measurement, power consumption, and particle contact information are used for obtaining a better understanding of the wear behavior and its effects on grinding mechanisms. Data from a vertical stirred mill screw liner wear measurement obtained in a full-scale mill are used to correlate with simulation results. The results indicate a relative agreement with industrial measurement in most of the liner lifecycle, when using a proper mill velocity scale-up.

## pqac-00000005

From text 'owen2009predictionofscrew pages 1-2'.

P.J. Owen and P.W. Cleary. Prediction of screw conveyor performance using the discrete element method (dem). Powder Technology, 193:274-288, Aug 2009. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.powtec.2009.03.012, doi:10.1016/j.powtec.2009.03.012. This article has 377 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt describes a DEM approach for screw-conveyor simulation in which particle motion and collisions with other particles, the casing, and the rotating screw are explicitly modeled. The geometry is created in CAD and imported into the DEM software as a triangular surface mesh, while particles are represented as spheres. To reduce the modeled domain, the study uses a single-pitch, standard-pitch screw with periodic boundary conditions; the reported geometry has a 38 mm screw diameter and pitch, a 13 mm shaft, approximately 1 mm blade thickness, and a 40 mm casing diameter. The simulations vary operating conditions including screw rotational speed, conveyor inclination, and volumetric fill level, and evaluate particle speed, mass flow rate, energy dissipation, and power consumption. The excerpt identifies the DEM code through references to Cleary’s work but does not name the software package. It also provides no details here about the particle contact law, friction or restitution parameters, cohesion model, computational hardware, runtime, or computational cost. Although the paper’s stated scope includes quantitative mass-flow predictions and comparison with prior experiments and empirical equations, these pages do not report numerical mass-flow rates or experimental-validation results. The cited prior studies include Shimizu and Cundall and Roberts and Willis.

## pqac-00000006

From text 'mcbride2009aninvestigationand pages 5-6'.

W. McBride and P.W. Cleary. An investigation and optimization of the ‘olds’ elevator using discrete element modeling. Powder Technology, 193:216-234, Aug 2009. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.powtec.2009.03.014, doi:10.1016/j.powtec.2009.03.014. This article has 72 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt describes a DEM approach for an OLDS screw elevator/conveyor. Particles were modeled as spheres or super-quadrics, with shape controlled by aspect ratios and the super-quadric power; super-quadrics require roughly 2–5 times the computational cost of equivalent sphere simulations. The CSIRO DEM code was used, with CAD geometry generated in PTC Pro/Engineer and transferred through STL. Neighbor searching used a periodically rebuilt search grid, reducing contact-detection work to O(N). Contacts between particles and boundaries were evaluated using a local spring-dashpot contact model, after which forces and torques were summed and integrated with a second-order predictor–corrector method. Time steps were typically 10^-4 to 10^-6 s, with at least 15 steps per collision. Numerical stiffness was deliberately reduced for efficiency: 1000 N/m for sorghum and 250 N/m for wheat; reported average overlaps were 0.17% and 0.15%. The excerpt does not specify a separate cohesion model or quantitative cohesion parameters. Validation involved matching the experimental test rig and comparing simulated flow behavior, while two internal measurement planes recorded upward flow and discharge rates. However, this excerpt does not provide the achieved numerical mass-flow rates or detailed experimental-versus-DEM validation errors.

## pqac-00000007

From text 'arthur2024processsimulationof pages 17-18'.

Tony Bediako Arthur and Nejat Rahmanian. Process simulation of twin-screw granulation: a review. Pharmaceutics, 16:706, May 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/pharmaceutics16060706, doi:10.3390/pharmaceutics16060706. This article has 1 citations.

The excerpt reports DEM applications to twin-screw granulators and twin-screw feeders. For the granulator, simulations used the commercial EDEM 2017 software, with geometry built from real-scale CAD data. Particle adhesion/cohesion was represented using the Johnson–Kendall–Roberts (JKR) theory, while the Hertz–Mindlin contact model represented normal and tangential forces. The model was combined with experiments and agreed with measured mixing diffusion coefficients at different screw speeds, providing experimental validation of particle movement. It predicted that increasing screw speed reduced average residence time and fill level, whereas increasing fill level increased compressive force and ultimately granule strength. For the feeder, DEM was used to examine residence-time distribution, discharge, refill mixing, and material tracking. Three approaches were compared: an exponential RTD/perfect-mixing model, an RTD model derived from DEM, and particle-level tracking using a “relay race” extrapolation. Perfect mixing was adequate for refills at or below 30% fill level; higher fill levels required the more detailed RTD or relay-race models. The excerpt does not provide computational costs, runtimes, hardware requirements, mass-flow rates, or feeder mass-throughput validation data.

## pqac-00000008

From text 'mcbride2009aninvestigationand pages 18-19'.

W. McBride and P.W. Cleary. An investigation and optimization of the ‘olds’ elevator using discrete element modeling. Powder Technology, 193:216-234, Aug 2009. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.powtec.2009.03.014, doi:10.1016/j.powtec.2009.03.014. This article has 72 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

This excerpt reports conclusions from 3D discrete-element simulations of the OLDS elevator and comparisons with experiments. The simulated mass-flow rates agreed very well with experimental measurements, supporting quantitatively accurate DEM prediction when particle and machine geometries are represented accurately. For the tested granular materials, OLDS flow rate was approximately linear with shroud rotational speed, suggesting use as a vertical feeder and enabling repeated batch delivery by counting shroud revolutions. The excerpt does not provide numerical absolute mass-flow rates, nor does it identify the DEM software, integration scheme, contact law, particle-contact parameters, cohesion model, hardware, runtime, or computational cost. It does provide comparative throughput information for screw geometry: a 5% radial clearance produced approximately 90% of the close-fitting screw’s flow rate, while 10% clearance produced approximately 85%. Increasing bed depth left axial velocity relatively unchanged, while total mass flow appeared to approach an asymptotic value, interpreted as increasing average conveyor density. The passage also notes that particle shape dominates friction in controlling shear resistance, and that elongated wheat particles exhibit stronger interlocking and reduced recirculation. Tall cutters generated substantial localized bed upheaval, whereas lower cutters caused less disturbance.

However, this excerpt does not identify the DEM software, integration or simulation method details, particle–wall or particle–particle contact models, cohesion models, timestep or computational-cost requirements, or the numerical mass-flow rates achieved. The broader introduction notes that screw-conveyor behavior depends on screw geometry, rotational speed, feeding method, and bulk-material properties, and that conventional theoretical methods may be unreliable for unusual materials or screw designs. More detailed information about modeling assumptions, calibration, computational expense, mass-flow results, and experimental validation would need to be obtained from later sections of the article or other cited studies.

Abstract:
The screw conveyor with no overlap between two screw blades and the screw conveyor with large overlap between two screw blades were simulated by discrete element method and the distribution of particle axial velocity, angular velocity, forces around the shell and forces around screw blades was carried out. The results show that: the screw conveyor with no overlap between two screw blades has better performance, because its average axial velocity of particles and conveying capacity are larger, its mean angular velocity of particles and forces around screw blades and the shell are smaller and its power consumption is also less; Particles around the bottom of the shell and the edge of screw blades are more prone to be worn-out and break up; Forces around the bottom of the shell and the edge of screw blades are larger, so double screw conveyors will most probable be destroyed in these two positions. The above results can provide references for structures selection and optimal design of double screw conveyors. Keywords—double screw conveyors; discrete element method; velocity distribution; forces distribution; structure optimization

Abstract:
The mechanism that carries the powder or tiny granular particles with the rotational movement of the spiral shaft is called the screw conveyor. The working principle of screw conveyors is transporting dust particles due to rotating the screw shaft placed in a cylindrical pipe with engine power. The transport process transfers the powder particles to the conveyor from the feed pipe at the top of the mechanism to the wings (helix) of the helix shaft. In this study, a scaled prototype of the screw conveyor was produced. Different Bayburt stone (Tüfit) sizes were transported utilizing the prototype, and natural frequency changes were measured during transportation. Consequently, it is observed that the different micron sizes of stone particles affect the natural frequency of the screw conveyor.

Bilal El-Kassem, Nizar Salloum, Thomas Brinz, Yousef Heider, and Bernd Markert. A multivariate regression parametric study on dem input parameters of free-flowing and cohesive powders with experimental data-based validation. Computational Particle Mechanics, 8:87-111, Jan 2020. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s40571-020-00315-8, doi:10.1007/s40571-020-00315-8. This article has 43 citations.

The excerpt identifies the DEM parameters investigated but does not provide the numerical parameter values for AlSi10Mg, 316L stainless steel, Ti-6Al-4V, or cohesive fine powders. The study used Young’s modulus (Y), Poisson’s ratio (ν), particle–particle static friction coefficient (µs,pp), particle–particle rolling friction coefficient (µr,pp), restitution coefficient (epp), and cohesion energy density as key particle properties. Hertz–Mindlin contact and EPSD2 rolling-friction models were applied to both free-flowing and dry cohesive powders, while the SJKR adhesion model was added for cohesive powders. Wall and funnel material properties were selected from literature, whereas several particle parameters were calibrated or estimated because direct microscale measurements were difficult. Specifically, µs,pp was measured using an FT4 powder rheometer but calibrated after reducing Young’s modulus for computational reasons; epp and µr,pp were tuned to reproduce bulk behavior; and cohesion energy density was estimated through preliminary screening simulations. The numerical values presumably appear in Table 2 or elsewhere in the full article, but they are not included in the supplied pages 7–9 excerpt.

Abstract:
In pharmaceutical manufacturing, the utmost aim is reliably producing high quality products. Simulation approaches allow virtual experiments of processes in the planning phase and the implementation of digital twins in operation. The industrial processing of active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) into tablets requires the combination of discrete and continuous sub-processes with complex interdependencies regarding the material structures and characteristics. The API and excipients are mixed, granulated if required, and subsequently tableted. Thereby, the structure as well as the properties of the intermediate and final product are influenced by the raw materials, the parametrized processes and environmental conditions, which are subject to certain fluctuations. In this study, for the first time, an agent-based simulation model is presented, which enables the prediction, tracking, and tracing of resulting structures and properties of the intermediates of an industrial tableting process. Therefore, the methodology for the identification and development of product and process agents in an agent-based simulation is shown. Implemented physical models describe the impact of process parameters on material structures. The tablet production with a pilot scale rotary press is experimentally characterized to provide calibration and validation data. Finally, the simulation results, predicting the final structures, are compared to the experimental data.

3. Model calibration

In order to calibrate the surface energy of the proposed DEM model, the angle of repose (AOR) has been determined
for powder piles resulting from experimental and numerical funnel tests. To measure the AOR experimentally, powder
was dispensed through a funnel with a discharge opening of 1mm diameter and a cone angle of 60◦onto the center of a
cube with side length a=a0 =10mm placed below the opening of the funnel. The (ﬁxed) distance between the center of
the cube and the opening of the funnel has been chosen as small as possible for each powder type to limit the powder
impact velocity. The test was concluded when the powder pile covered the entire surface of the cube such that further
addition of powder would result in no additional accumulation of powder. While the angle of repose is a well-deﬁned
metric of noncohesive granular materials, the angle of repose measured for highly cohesive powders might depend on
the deformation history as well as on the problem size, which inﬂuences e.g. its avalanching behavior [9]. To address
the problem of history dependence, it has been ensured in experiments and simulations that the powder is initially
in a ”loose” state, i.e. that it is not pre-compressed. In order to study the sensitivity with respect to problem size,
additional experiments with down-scaled variants of the problem setup (cube with side lengths a = a0/2 = 5mm and
a=a0/4=2.5mm at unchanged discharge opening) have been conducted. Moreover, three powders with diﬀerent par-
ticle size distributions (PSD) have been employed in the experimental funnel studies discussed in the following. These
are a medium-sized powder typical for SLM applications (D10 = 20µm, D50 = 34µm, D90 = 44µm, mean diameter
¯d = 34µm), a rather coarse-grained powder (D10 = 46µm, D50 = 72µm, D90 = 106µm, mean diameter ¯d = 72µm) as
well as a rather ﬁne-grained powder (D10 = 8µm, D50 = 14µm, D90 = 23µm, mean diameter ¯d = 14µm).

In the numerical tests, the problem scaling a=a0/4 has been considered to limit the computational costs. Furthermore,
all numerical simulations within this work are based on a powder particle size distribution ﬁtting the medium-sized
powder (¯d = 34µm). In order to enable accurate AOR measurements also for the down-scaled numerical variant, it
is desirable to keep the curved region at the particle impact zone on the top of the powder pile as small as possible,
which can be achieved by reducing the powder mass ﬂow and impact velocity, and thus the resulting impact momen-
tum. In the numerical simulations, this is realized by driving down the cube during the ﬂow experiments to limit the
drop height of the particles. Furthermore, the diameter of the discharge opening has been decreased to 0.4mm, and
the adhesion between powder particles and the funnel walls has been switched oﬀ(while adhesion between particles
and the cube is an important system property and has been kept) in order to ensure continuous powder ﬂow even for
this smaller opening. For the experimental and numerical analysis of very ﬁne / cohesive powders, an additional small
vibration amplitude has been applied to the funnel in order to increase ﬂowability. It has been veriﬁed that all these
modiﬁcations mainly inﬂuence the shape and relative size of the curved impact zone on the top of the powder pile
without having noticeable inﬂuence on the angle of repose measured on the ﬂanks of the pile. The initial and ﬁnal
conﬁguration of the numerical problem setup is illustrated in Figure 2.

Figure 3 illustrates the 2D projections of the powder piles resulting from these numerical simulations for diﬀerent
choices of the surface energy γ. Based on these 2D images, the AOR values have been measured by ﬁtting an equi-
lateral triangle (green dashed lines) for each powder pile. As expected, the angle of repose increases with increasing

trostatic potentials, and van der Waals (vdW) interactions. The latter term commonly refers to the accumulated eﬀects
resulting from so-called Keesom forces (interaction of two permanent dipoles), Debeye forces (interaction of a per-
manent and an induced dipole) as well as London dispersion forces (interaction of polarizable but initially non-polar
molecules). Since metal powder fusion processes such as SLM require the powder humidity level to be as low as

required for the subsequent modeling of vdW interactions, and are in strong analogy to the review article by Wal-

Abstract:
Highly potent active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) and low-dose excipients, or excipients with very low density, are notoriously hard to feed with currently available commercial technology. The micro-feeder system presented in this work is capable of feeding low-dose rates of powders with different particle sizes and flow properties. Two different grades of lactose, di-calcium phosphate, croscarmellose sodium, silicon dioxide, a spray-dried intermediate, and an active ingredient were studied to vary material properties to test performance of the system. The current micro-feeder system is a volumetric feeder combined with a weighing balance at the outlet that measures feeder output rates. Feeding results are shown as a so-called “displacement-feed factor” curve for each material. Since the powder mass and volume are known in the micro-feeder system, in this work, we characterized an observed density variation during processing via a “displacement-feed factor” profile for each of the fed powders. This curve can be later used for calibrating the system to ensure an accurate, constant feed rate and in addition predicting feeding performance for that material at any feed rate. There is a relation between powder properties and feeding performance. Powders with finer particles and higher compressibility show densification during their feeding process. However, powders with larger particles and lower compressibility show both “densification” and “powder bed expansion,” which is the manifestation of dilation and elastic recovery of particles during the micro-feeding process. Through the application of the displacement-feed factor, it is possible to provide precise feeding accuracy of low-dose materials.

From text 'bascone2020hybridmechanisticempiricalapproach pages 4-8'.

Davide Bascone, Federico Galvanin, Nilay Shah, and Salvador Garcia-Munoz. Hybrid mechanistic-empirical approach to the modeling of twin screw feeders for continuous tablet manufacturing. Industrial & Engineering Chemistry Research, 59:6650-6661, Mar 2020. URL: https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.iecr.0c00420, doi:10.1021/acs.iecr.0c00420. This article has 16 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt identifies several reduced-order, analytical, and semi-empirical approaches for predicting screw-feeder mass flow from powder and equipment properties. Statistical or data-driven models, including response surfaces, kriging, multivariate methods, relative standard deviation, and ANOVA, relate feeder performance to cohesion, particle descriptors, compressibility, rheology, flow, permeability, porosity, tooling, powder, and screw speed. Boukouvala et al. proposed a first-order delay model in which mass flow responds dynamically to screw speed, with fitted delay and gain parameters. Escotet-Espinoza et al. developed a pressure-dependent feed-factor model: hopper powder mass determines the feed factor, defined as solids contained in one screw-pitch volume, and mass flow is estimated from feed factor multiplied by screw speed. This is closely related to a displacement or volumetric feed-factor concept, since it represents the quantity displaced per screw revolution. Yu, Arnold, and Roberts used analytical volumetric-efficiency models accounting for vortex motion and screw fullness; multiplying efficiency by bulk density, screw speed, and screw volume per pitch gives mass flow. The featured hybrid model combines hopper stress, pressure-dependent powder densification/effective density, screw geometry, and vortex-related volumetric efficiency, making it applicable to different powders and feeder geometries. Volumetric feeding is modeled directly, while gravimetric operation can use these relations within feedback control.

## pqac-00000022

From text 'bascone2020hybridmechanisticempiricalapproach pages 8-11'.

Davide Bascone, Federico Galvanin, Nilay Shah, and Salvador Garcia-Munoz. Hybrid mechanistic-empirical approach to the modeling of twin screw feeders for continuous tablet manufacturing. Industrial & Engineering Chemistry Research, 59:6650-6661, Mar 2020. URL: https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.iecr.0c00420, doi:10.1021/acs.iecr.0c00420. This article has 16 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt describes a hybrid mechanistic-empirical, reduced-order model for twin-screw feeders. Its steady or level mass-flow prediction is based on screw geometry, effective powder density, and an overall volumetric efficiency: ṁlevel = nPAρe(t)η. The geometry term captures the displacement capacity associated with screw starts, pitch, and available cross-sectional area, making it conceptually related to a displacement feed factor. However, the model does not treat displacement alone as sufficient: the effective density is time-dependent and is influenced by vertical stress along the hopper, thereby representing powder densification and degree of fill. The efficiency term includes a theoretical vortex-motion efficiency, ηv, calculated from friction coefficient and wall-friction angle, multiplied by the degree of fill, ηf. Dynamic behavior is represented separately with a First Order Plus Dead Time model, including a time constant and dead time; the delayed actual flow is distinguished from the initially reached level flow. Thus, the framework connects powder properties to volumetric feeding through friction, stress, density, and fill effects, and then predicts mass flow by multiplying volumetric capacity by effective density. The excerpt does not explicitly use the term “feed factor” or present a gravimetric-control model, but its geometry-times-density-times-efficiency formulation provides a mechanistic basis for such a factor and distinguishes instantaneous volumetric capacity from delayed mass-flow response.

The excerpt identifies a hybrid mechanistic–empirical first-order-plus-dead-time (FOPDT) model for twin-screw feeders. It is intended to predict dynamic feeder behavior using different powders and screw geometries, rather than providing a purely first-principles analytical expression for mass flow from powder properties. The stated motivation is that powder bulk-solid physics remains insufficiently understood, so feeder behavior is often treated as a black-box process and data-driven approaches such as response surfaces or kriging have also been used. The excerpt emphasizes that powder properties—including cohesion, particle descriptors, and compressibility—can significantly affect feeder performance, which is directly relevant to any feed-factor or reduced-order model based on material characteristics. Mechanistically, the screws function as a conveying mechanism, while mass flow is regulated by screw speed. In gravimetric operation, continuous weighing closes the loop and screw speed is adjusted to correct the mass flow rate. During hopper refill, the feeder operates volumetrically in open loop, with flow inferred from screw displacement/speed rather than continuously corrected by weight. The provided pages do not explicitly define a displacement-feed-factor equation, a powder-densification law, or a standalone analytical mass-flow model. They therefore support relating reduced-order modeling to volumetric versus gravimetric operation, but not specifying the mathematical form or parameterization of displacement factors or densification.

The excerpt presents reduced-order, analytical throughput models for screw feeders. The basic approach treats mass flow as the product of the screw’s conveying volume, powder density, and rotational speed. Feed capacity is first written as ṁp = FρVC, where F is the cross-sectional area of the feed layer, ρ is bulk-feed density, V is axial feed velocity, and C is an inclination correction factor. The filling area is represented by F = φA, with φ as the loading or filling coefficient; axial velocity is V = Pω, where P is screw pitch and ω is rotational speed. Combining these gives a theoretical capacity proportional to (D²−d²)Pρω, then adds correction factors C and φ for inclination, loading, and powder flowability. A second formulation replaces these corrections with volumetric efficiency ηv, giving a mass-flow estimate proportional to D²Pρηvω. Thus, powder properties enter primarily through bulk density, flowability, and the filling/loading or volumetric-efficiency factors. The excerpt does not explicitly identify a displacement-feed-factor model or a powder-densification law, but its filling coefficient, bulk density, and volumetric efficiency are potential reduced-order representations of incomplete filling and consolidation. These equations are principally volumetric screw-feeder models converted to mass flow using density, rather than explicitly gravimetric dynamic models.

The excerpt does not present a screw-feeder mass-flow model, analytical equation, or reduced-order model that predicts flow rate directly from powder properties. Instead, it describes an empirical calibration framework for a high-precision micro-feeder. The device uses advanced volumetric displacement—controlled piston movement in a powder-filled cartridge—and a weighing balance at the outlet to measure the resulting mass flow. Because both powder displacement/volume and mass are known, the authors define a material-specific “displacement-feed factor” profile that captures density changes during feeding. This profile can be used to calibrate the feeder for an accurate constant feed rate and to predict performance at other feed rates. The observed factor depends on powder properties: fine, more compressible powders tend to densify, whereas larger, less compressible particles can exhibit both densification and powder-bed expansion caused by dilation and elastic recovery. Thus, the approach is a phenomenological reduced calibration relationship rather than a mechanistic screw-feeder model. The text contrasts this precision volumetric method with conventional loss-in-weight gravimetric feeders, which generally handle larger, better-flowing powders at higher rates and may experience deviations during refill when operating temporarily in volumetric mode. Variability in packing density is identified as a key limitation of purely volumetric feeding.

The excerpt does not present a standalone analytical feed-factor or reduced-order model for predicting screw-feeder mass flow from powder properties. The discussion nevertheless provides relationships relevant to feed-factor modeling. Fill fraction determines the active cross-sectional area available for conveying; at a fixed mass flow rate, a larger fill fraction produces a lower mean inlet velocity. The conveying and compression behavior are coupled to density, strain rate, and yield stress. Higher compression increases density and can increase torque, while the pressure-dependent density model predicts densification through the feeder. A dense plug may form in the compression zone and contribute to jamming or plugging. Thus, the excerpt supports a conceptual distinction between volumetric and gravimetric feeding: mass flow depends on volumetric transport combined with local bulk density, while gravimetric measurements provide the target mass flow used to set velocity and fill conditions. This excerpt does not develop analytical, reduced-order, or feed-factor models specifically for screw feeders. It does provide related concepts for displacement-based powder feeding. The study evaluates a high-precision low-dose feeder in which powder is displaced and the discharged mass is recorded gravimetrically. Its key quantity, the “relative effective displacement density” (ρ*ED), represents the powder mass associated with the displaced volume relative to a reference density. The excerpt states that feed rate equals ρ*ED multiplied by displaced volume per unit time, linking volumetric displacement to mass flow. Thus, ρ*ED functions conceptually like a displacement feed factor: it converts geometric displacement into mass flow while accounting for the powder’s current bulk density. The measurements show that powder properties strongly affect this factor. Fine, cohesive powders such as GranuLac200 and croscarmellose sodium exhibit increasing feed rate and effective density during feeding, attributed to pre-conditioning gradients and/or densification caused by wall friction. Other materials show initial expansion followed by densification. These observations are relevant to volumetric-versus-gravimetric feeding because a fixed displacement or screw volume does not necessarily produce constant mass flow when powder density evolves. However, the excerpt supplies empirical observations rather than a general screw-feeder predictive model.

Abstract:
This study first reviewed theories of the mechanical response of structures under loading, and the discrete element method provides a route for studying mechanical response including elastic deformation and structure failure. However, the direct acquisition of the microscopic parameters from the governing equations of the discrete element method via experiments encounters challenges. One possible strategy to obtain these microscopic parameters is parameter calibration that are widely used by researchers. Secondly, the governing equations and failure criterion of the discrete element method are summarized, and the microscopic parameters that would be calibrated are pinpointed. Next, the principles of classical calibration methods of discrete element method are explicated in detail, alongside the validation and discussion of their properties. Lastly, this study examined the applicability of calibrated parameters and points out that the size ratio, porosity, maximum radius, and minimum radius of particles should be identical in both the geometric calibration model and that for applications.

## 1. Mapping snow avalanches hazard in poorly monitored areas. The case of Rigopiano avalanche, Apennines of Italy
Valid Text Names:
'bocchiola2018mappingsnowavalanches pages 1-3', 'bocchiola2018mappingsnowavalanches pages 3-6', 'bocchiola2018mappingsnowavalanches pages 6-8', 'bocchiola2018mappingsnowavalanches pages 8-10', 'bocchiola2018mappingsnowavalanches pages 10-17', 'bocchiola2018mappingsnowavalanches pages 17-21', 'bocchiola2018mappingsnowavalanches pages 21-26', 'bocchiola2018mappingsnowavalanches pages 26-29', 'bocchiola2018mappingsnowavalanches pages 29-31', 'bocchiola2018mappingsnowavalanches pages 31-31'

BibTex:
@article{bocchiola2018mappingsnowavalanches,
    author = "Bocchiola, Daniele and Galizzi, Mattia and Bombelli, Giovanni Martino and Soncini, Andrea",
    title = "Mapping snow avalanches hazard in poorly monitored areas. The case of Rigopiano avalanche, Apennines of Italy",
    year = "2018",
    journal = "Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences",
    pages = "1-31",
    month = "Dec",
    doi = "10.5194/nhess-2018-358",
    url = "https://doi.org/10.5194/nhess-2018-358",
    publisher = "Copernicus GmbH"
}


Abstract:
Abstract. Hazard mapping is carried out in Italy according to the AINEVA guidelines, which require (i) data driven avalanche dynamic modelling to assess end mark and pressure, and (ii) assessment of maximum yearly three-day snow depth increase h72 for 30 to 300 years return period. When no historical avalanche data are present, model tuning and data based assessment of avalanche return periods are hardly feasible. Also when (very) short series of h72 are available, station based quantile estimation for such high return periods is very uncertain, and regionally based approaches can be used. We apply an index value approach for the case study avalanche of Rigopiano, where a 105 m3 snow mass hit the Rigopiano Hotel killing 29 persons on January 18th 2017. This area is poorly monitored avalanche wise, and displays short series (max 14 years) of snow depth measurements, no historical avalanche maps are available on the avalanche track, and no hazard maps have been developed hitherto. First, we tune the recently developed Poly-Aval dynamic avalanche model (1D/q2D) against the 18th January event data (release zone, release depth, end mark) from different sources. We then use snow data from 7 snow stations in Abruzzo (75 equivalent years of data) to tune a regionally valid distribution of h72. We then calculate the 30-years, 100-years, and 300-years runout zone and flow pressures, including confidence limits. We demonstrate that (i) properly tuned 1D/quasi2D models can be used for avalanche modeling even within poorly monitored area as here, and (ii) the use of regional analysis allows hazard mapping for large return periods, reducing greatly the uncertainty against canonical, single site analysis. Our approach is usable in poorly monitored regions like Abruzzo here, and we suggest that (i) avalanche hazard mapping needs to be pursued with regional approaches for h72, and (ii) confidence limits need to be provided for the proposed zoning.

URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s40571-020-00315-8, doi:10.1007/s40571-020-00315-8. This article has 43 citations.

The excerpt describes coarse-graining as the principal method used to reduce DEM computational expense. In this approach, original particles of radius R are replaced with larger particles of radius R′, obtained by multiplying the original radius by a scaling factor Sf. Interaction laws and equations of motion are adjusted according to scaling rules so that gravitational potential-energy density, kinetic-energy density, and energy dissipation per volume and time are preserved. Particle density remains fixed; each coarse-grained particle’s mass increases by Sf3, while the number of particles decreases by the same factor, conserving total mass. The method is reported to save significant computational time and produce acceptable bulk-property agreement, although it cannot reproduce the exact heap shape. For angle-of-repose simulations, coarse-graining had no considerable effect on the resulting angles. The excerpt does not mention screw feeders specifically, reduced Young’s modulus, GPU acceleration, or quantitative computational-cost reductions. It only states that simulations were run on an eight-node cluster using 32 Intel Xeon CPUs, and that Young’s modulus was selected as a fixed material parameter rather than reduced as an acceleration technique.

function.arguments: {"artifact_type": "table", "description": "Create a comprehensive comparison table of physics-based simulation methods used to model screw/auger feeders and micro-dosing of powders. Include columns for: Method, Software/Code, Contact/Cohesion Model, Speed-ups Used, Typical Computational Cost, Validated Against, Studies Using Inverse Inference. Include the following methods: 1) DEM with Hertz-Mindlin + SJKR (LIGGGHTS), 2) DEM with linear spring-dashpot (CSIRO code), 3) DEM with Hertz-Mindlin + JKR (EDEM), 4) DEM with Hertz-Mindlin + JKR (general/other codes), 5) Coupled CFD-DEM, 6) Continuum Eulerian CFD, 7) Analytical/Reduced-order feed-factor models."}

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-00)

| Method | Software / code | Contact / cohesion model | Speed-ups used | Typical computational cost | Validated against experiments | Studies using inverse inference from feeder data |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| DEM: Hertz–Mindlin + SJKR | **LIGGGHTS**; applicable also in LAMMPS-derived granular implementations | Hertz–Mindlin normal/tangential contact; Coulomb sliding; modified simplified JKR force, `F_coh = C·A_contact`; EPSD2 rolling resistance. Published cohesive-powder screening used cohesion-energy density `C_pp = 30–70 kJ m⁻³` (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018) | Reduced Young’s modulus; coarse-graining with particle radius scaled by `S_f`, particle mass by `S_f³`, and count reduced correspondingly; domain trimming; MPI parallelism. Coarse-graining preserved angle of repose reasonably but not exact heap geometry (pqac-00000029) | Strongly particle-count and stiffness dependent. The user’s millimetre auger requires **26–30 CPU-min per revolution**; published powder calibration campaigns require tens of full runs (40 noncohesive; 53 cohesive) on multicore hardware (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000029) | Angle of repose, porosity, mass-flow rate and bulk density in powder-calibration studies; screw studies commonly target throughput, inclination/speed response, torque and power. AOR is most often used for cohesion/friction calibration rather than feeder output (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000013) | **No published feeder-data Bayesian inversion identified.** El-Kassem et al. used design of experiments and multivariate regression, not Bayesian inference; parameters were calibrated to bulk AOR/porosity/flow responses (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000018) |
| DEM: linear spring–dashpot | **CSIRO in-house DEM code** used by Cleary, Owen and McBride | Linear normal and tangential spring–dashpot contact with friction; spheres or superquadrics; no explicit cohesion in the cited screw-conveyor studies (pqac-00000006) | Periodic one-pitch domains; `O(N)` grid neighbour search; deliberately reduced stiffness (`250 N m⁻¹` for wheat; `1000 N m⁻¹` for sorghum); spheres instead of superquadrics. Superquadrics cost about 2–5× more than spheres (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006) | Explicit time steps typically `10⁻⁴–10⁻⁶ s`, with at least 15 steps per collision. Runtime was not reported; periodic single-pitch models substantially reduce particle count (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006) | Screw-conveyor mass flow, particle axial/swirl velocity, inclination and fill-level effects, power and energy dissipation; OLDS-elevator mass-flow predictions agreed very well with experiments. Vertical operation reduced volumetric transport by 23–47% relative to horizontal operation in one study (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000011) | **None identified.** These studies were forward prediction and engineering optimization, not inference of powder properties from feeder measurements |
| DEM: Hertz–Mindlin + JKR | **EDEM** (commercial) | Hertz–Mindlin normal/tangential contact; Mindlin–Deresiewicz tangential response; Coulomb friction; rolling resistance; JKR surface-energy adhesion. Setting surface energy to zero recovers noncohesive Hertz contact (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000007) | Reduced modulus/stiffness, simplified spherical particles, limited geometry and prescribed inlet throughput are common; GPU acceleration is available in modern EDEM, but quantitative speed-up was not reported in the cited feeder/granulator studies | Usually hours to days for realistic twin-screw equipment; exact runtimes were not reported. Cost rises sharply for true 10–100 μm PSDs and for refill simulations requiring long residence times | Twin-screw mixing diffusion coefficient, mean residence-time trends, fill level, refill mixing and residence-time distribution; feeder studies examined discharge and refill, with perfect-mixing approximations adequate only at ≤30% fill in the cited analysis (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000007) | **No feeder-based Bayesian inference identified.** Published work calibrates JKR surface energy or friction to AOR/dynamic-yield-strength tests and then validates residence-time or mixing behavior (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002) |
| DEM: Hertz–Mindlin + JKR or adhesive pull-off law | **Rocky, PFC, MercuryDPM, Yade, Project Chrono, Blaze-DEM**, and research codes; direct screw-feeder evidence is strongest for EDEM and in-house codes, while the others are established DEM options rather than well-documented micro-auger precedents (pqac-00000003) | Hertz–Mindlin with JKR; alternatively regularized van der Waals/pull-off force plus sliding friction and rolling resistance. For 34 μm Ti-6Al-4V, effective surface energy `γ = 0.1 mJ m⁻²`; a useful metal-powder prior is approximately `0.1–1 mJ m⁻²` (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000037) | GPU solvers in Rocky, Chrono and Blaze-DEM; reduced modulus; periodic sectors; sphere or multisphere approximations; coarse-graining. Shape-resolved particles improve interlocking but increase cost | GPU DEM can reduce wall time substantially, but no transferable feeder runtime was reported. Fully resolved 10–30 μm powders remain expensive because stable time step and particle count both worsen | Metal-powder AOR, Hall-type discharge, powder-bed packing, roughness and spreading; Ti-6Al-4V cohesion was inferred by matching simulated and experimental AOR, not from an auger (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000036, pqac-00000037) | **Bulk-test inverse calibration only.** Meier et al. fitted effective surface energy to AOR; this is deterministic calibration rather than Bayesian feeder inversion (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000016) |
| Coupled CFD–DEM | **MFiX-DEM**, LIGGGHTS–OpenFOAM/CFDEM, EDEM–CFD, Fluent–DEM; no strong published precedent was located for a dry, slowly rotating 3 mm micro-auger | DEM contact laws as above plus gas–particle drag, pressure-gradient and possibly lift forces; cohesion can use JKR/SJKR, although coarse-graining must also preserve drag and cohesion similarity | Particle coarse-graining; CFD mesh coarsening; unresolved fluid cells; GPU DEM; reduced stiffness. Simply enlarging particles without consistent coarse-graining can give erroneous, overly rapid filling because air drag changes (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030) | Typically several times more expensive than dry DEM at the same particle count; practical runs range from hours to days. Additional expense is justified when aeration, pneumatic assistance, gas leakage or fine-powder entrainment materially affects flow | In related powder-processing work: filling dynamics, pressure/airflow, suspension velocity and mixing. Direct validation of micro-auger dose increments, no-flow events, taps or afterflow was not identified (pqac-00000030) | **None identified for feeder data.** A future inverse model could infer permeability or effective drag jointly with cohesion, but identifiability would require pressure or airflow observations in addition to balance data |
| Continuum Eulerian granular CFD | Research CFD and commercial solvers such as **OpenFOAM, Fluent or COMSOL**; the cited compression-feed-screw work used a compressible continuum framework (pqac-00000027) | Compressible granular continuum with pressure-dependent density, yield stress and strain-rate dependence; possible frictional-plastic, Drucker–Prager/Mohr–Coulomb or `μ(I)` closures. No particle contact law is resolved | Fixed Eulerian mesh; steady or rotating-reference formulations; reduced-order constitutive laws; much lower degrees of freedom than particle-resolved DEM | Commonly minutes to hours per operating point, depending on mesh and moving-boundary treatment; far cheaper than true-size DEM, but constitutive calibration dominates uncertainty | Pressure, torque, densification, plug formation and mean throughput in compression screws. Evidence for validating milligram-scale increment fluctuations, individual taps, afterflow or zero-flow probability is lacking (pqac-00000027) | **No feeder-based Bayesian property inference identified.** In principle suitable for inferring bulk yield locus, compressibility and wall friction, but not unique particle-scale surface energy or restitution |
| Analytical / reduced-order feed-factor models | Spreadsheet, MATLAB/Python, process simulators and control-system implementations; no DEM code required | Mass flow represented by screw displacement × effective density × speed × fill/volumetric efficiency. Hybrid models add hopper stress, pressure-dependent densification, vortex efficiency and first-order-plus-dead-time dynamics: `ṁ = nPAρ_eη` (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000024) | Intrinsically reduced order; fitted feed-factor curves, response surfaces, Gaussian-process/kriging surrogates and state-space/FOPDT models enable real-time prediction and control | Milliseconds per evaluation; calibration requires experimental sweeps but posterior sampling is inexpensive | Steady and dynamic mass flow, screw-speed response, hopper-level dependence, density drift, refill transients and low-dose precision. Displacement-feed-factor experiments explicitly captured powder densification, dilation and elastic recovery (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000028) | **Best-established route for operational parameter estimation, but generally empirical rather than physics-identifying.** Published models fit gains, delays, effective density and efficiency; they do not uniquely recover cohesion or microscopic friction. They are well suited as emulators or discrepancy models around a smaller DEM training set (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000023) |

function.arguments: {"artifact_type": "table", "description": "Create a ranking table of simulation methods by suitability for a millimetre-scale auger dosing cohesive fine powders (10-100 \u00b5m) and salts. Include columns: Rank, Method, Suitability Rating (1-5 stars), Strengths for this application, Limitations for this application, Recommended Use Case. Rank from most to least suitable: 1) DEM with Hertz-Mindlin + SJKR/JKR cohesion (LIGGGHTS) - highest because it directly models particle contacts, cohesion, and the user already has a validated model; 2) DEM with JKR (EDEM/Rocky) - also excellent but commercial; 3) Analytical/reduced-order feed-factor models - fast, useful for control and surrogate; 4) Coupled CFD-DEM - useful if aeration matters; 5) Continuum Eulerian CFD - too coarse for milligram increments; 6) SPH/MPM - no published screw feeder precedent."}

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-02)

| Rank | Method | Suitability Rating | Strengths for this application | Limitations for this application | Recommended Use Case |
|---:|---|:---:|---|---|---|
| 1 | DEM with Hertz–Mindlin + SJKR/JKR cohesion (**LIGGGHTS**) | ★★★★★ | Resolves particle contacts, force chains, wall friction, rolling resistance, cohesion, outlet bridging, intermittent flow, tapping, and afterflow; directly predicts mass per revolution and zero-flow increments. The existing salt result provides unusually strong application-specific validation. LIGGGHTS supports Hertz–Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, EPSD2 rolling resistance, parallel execution, and coarse-graining (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000029) | True 10–100 µm particles require large particle counts and small time steps; SJKR cohesion-energy density is an effective, model-dependent parameter; coarse-graining can distort arching and outlet intermittency when coarse particles become too large relative to the 3 mm outlet | Primary calibration model. Retain the validated salt configuration, add moisture-conditioned cohesion and wall parameters, and train a surrogate for Bayesian inference from mass/revolution, taps, afterflow, and no-flow statistics |
| 2 | DEM with Hertz–Mindlin + JKR (**EDEM or Rocky**) | ★★★★☆ | JKR surface-energy adhesion is physically interpretable for fine powders; commercial preprocessing, moving geometry, particle-shape tools, and GPU solvers simplify parameter sweeps. EDEM studies have represented cohesive screw and twin-screw transport, mixing, residence time, discharge, and refill (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000007) | License cost and reduced reproducibility; inferred JKR surface energy is not numerically interchangeable with LIGGGHTS SJKR cohesion-energy density. True PSD and nonspherical particles remain expensive, and published validation is mainly for larger feeders or granulators rather than milligram doses | Best commercial cross-check or GPU alternative; useful for testing JKR versus SJKR, particle shape, refill mixing, and whether inferred parameters transfer between solvers |
| 3 | Analytical or reduced-order feed-factor models | ★★★★☆ | Evaluations take milliseconds and are therefore ideal for closed-loop control and Bayesian sampling. Models combine screw displacement, speed, effective density, filling efficiency, hopper stress, densification, and first-order/dead-time dynamics; displacement-feed-factor measurements capture densification and dilation (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000028) | Parameters such as effective density, efficiency, gain, and time constant are lumped quantities; they generally cannot uniquely identify microscopic cohesion, sliding friction, or rolling friction. Bridging, taps, and stochastic no-flow increments require additional state or hurdle models | Real-time digital twin and control model; use as the emulator/discrepancy layer around a limited DEM design, with separate probabilistic models for no-flow events and tap-released mass |
| 4 | Coupled CFD–DEM | ★★★☆☆ | Adds gas pressure, permeability, drag, aeration, and entrainment while retaining particle contacts and cohesion. It may explain speed-dependent fluidization, powder puffing, humidity-conditioned permeability, or delayed settling that dry DEM misses | More expensive and less identifiable than dry DEM; gas coupling is probably secondary at 1–30 rpm unless very fine, low-density, or aerated powders are used. Coarse-graining must preserve both contact and drag similarity; simply enlarging particles can produce incorrect filling dynamics (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030) | Escalation model only when dry DEM leaves systematic residuals correlated with speed, powder permeability, density, outlet pressure, or air displacement; add pressure measurements before inferring drag parameters |
| 5 | Continuum Eulerian granular CFD with Drucker–Prager, Mohr–Coulomb, compressible-plastic, or μ(I) closure | ★★☆☆☆ | Far cheaper than particle-resolved DEM; suitable for mean stress, density, plug formation, torque, pressure, and average throughput. {"answer": "## Physics-Based Simulation Methods for Screw/Auger Feeders and Powder Micro-Dosing: A Comprehensive Review

### 1. Introduction

The simulation of screw and auger feeders for powder dosing has been approached through a range of physics-based methods spanning particle-resolved discrete element methods, coupled fluid-particle approaches, continuum formulations, and analytical reduced-order models. This review synthesizes the available literature to identify which methods, software codes, contact and cohesion models, speed-up strategies, and validation approaches have been employed, and ranks them by suitability for a millimetre-scale auger dosing cohesive fine powders (10–100 µm) and salts.

### 2. Discrete Element Method (DEM) — The Dominant Approach

DEM is by far the most widely used physics-based simulation method for screw feeders and powder dosing. It resolves individual particle contacts, force chains, wall friction, bridging, and intermittent flow that are critical for understanding dose-to-dose variability.

**2.1 DEM with Linear Spring-Dashpot Contact (CSIRO Code)**

Owen and Cleary (2009) used the CSIRO in-house DEM code to predict screw conveyor performance including particle speed, mass flow rate, energy dissipation, and power consumption (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011). They employed periodic one-pitch domains with a 38 mm diameter screw and studied the effects of screw speed (600–1400 rpm), inclination (0–90°), and fill level (30–70%). Mass flow rate decreased strongly and linearly with increasing inclination until about 60° and was reduced by 23–47% when operating vertically compared to horizontal (pqac-00000011). McBride and Cleary (2009) applied the same code to the OLDS elevator, using deliberately reduced contact stiffness (1000 N/m for sorghum, 250 N/m for wheat) to achieve computationally tractable time steps of 10⁻⁴–10⁻⁶ s with at least 15 steps per collision (pqac-00000006). Simulated mass-flow rates agreed very well with experiments, and flow rate was approximately linear with rotational speed (pqac-00000008). Super-quadric particle shapes were available but cost 2–5× more than equivalent sphere simulations (pqac-00000006).

**2.2 DEM with Hertz-Mindlin + SJKR Cohesion (LIGGGHTS)**

El-Kassem et al. (2021) conducted a systematic parametric study using LIGGGHTS with the Hertz-Mindlin contact model, the EPSD2 rolling resistance model, and the modified simplified Johnson-Kendall-Roberts (SJKR) cohesion model (pqac-00000017). The SJKR model adds a cohesive normal force F_coh = C·a to the Hertzian contact, where C is the cohesion energy density (J/m³) and a is the contact area (pqac-00000017). They investigated six DEM input parameters—Young's modulus, particle size, restitution coefficient, static friction, rolling friction, and cohesion energy density—and validated against angle of repose, porosity, and mass flow rate using free-flowing lactose (SpheroLac 100) and cohesive lactose (InhaLac 251) powders (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000018). For cohesive powders, the rolling friction coefficient had the most substantial impact on angle of repose, while static friction played a minor role (pqac-00000004). Simulations were run on an eight-node cluster using 32 Intel Xeon CPUs; coarse-graining with a scaling factor S_f was used, preserving energy density while reducing particle count by S_f³ (pqac-00000029).

**2.3 DEM with Hertz-Mindlin + JKR (EDEM and Other Commercial Codes)**

EDEM, the most widely used commercial DEM platform, employs the JKR surface-energy adhesion model where setting surface energy to zero recovers non-cohesive Hertz contact (pqac-00000002). Arthur and Rahmanian (2024) reviewed DEM applications to twin-screw granulators and feeders using EDEM with JKR cohesion, finding that simulations predicted mixing diffusion coefficients that agreed with experiments at different screw speeds (pqac-00000007). For feeders specifically, DEM was used to examine residence-time distribution, discharge, refill mixing, and material tracking, with perfect-mixing models adequate only at fill levels ≤30% (pqac-00000007). Rocky and PFC are also established commercial codes that support Hertz-Mindlin with JKR or similar adhesion models, with Rocky offering a GPU solver and realistic particle-shape libraries (pqac-00000003).

**2.4 DEM for Metal Powder Cohesion (AM-Focused)**

Meier et al. (2018) developed a DEM framework specifically for fine metal powders used in additive manufacturing, incorporating frictional contact, rolling resistance, and a regularized van der Waals adhesive pull-off force (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015). For plasma-atomized Ti-6Al-4V powder (mean diameter 34 µm), they calibrated an effective surface energy of γ₀ = 0.1 mJ/m² by matching simulated and experimental angle-of-repose tests (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000019). This effective value is orders of magnitude lower than theoretical metal surface energies (~1000 mJ/m²) and experimental flat-contact values (30–50 mJ/m²), attributed to surface roughness, contamination, and oxidation (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000020). They estimated that 0.1–1 mJ/m² is a plausible effective range for metal AM powders and found that angle of repose is more sensitive to surface energy than to particle stiffness, friction coefficient, or coefficient of restitution (pqac-00000037).

### 3. Coupled CFD-DEM

Coupled CFD-DEM adds gas-phase pressure, permeability, and drag forces to the particle-resolved framework. For screw conveyors, this approach has been applied primarily to pneumatic conveying and aeration-assisted systems rather than slow, dry micro-dosing. Coarse-graining in CFD-DEM must preserve both contact and drag similarity; simply enlarging particles without consistent coarse-graining produces erroneous, overly rapid filling because air drag effects change (pqac-00000030). No persuasive published precedent was identified for a dry, slowly rotating 3 mm micro-auger using CFD-DEM. The approach would be justified if aeration, gas leakage, or fine-powder entrainment materially affects flow at the operating speeds of 1–30 rpm.

### 4. Continuum Approaches

**4.1 Eulerian Granular CFD**

Continuum frameworks treating powder as a compressible granular fluid have been applied to compression-feed screws, where inlet velocity is prescribed from experimental mass flow rate, density, and fill fraction (pqac-00000027). The pressure-dependent density model predicts densification through the feeder, with dense plug formation contributing to jamming. However, a 3 mm outlet with 10–100 µm particles provides only tens of particle diameters across the opening, making continuum averaging inadequate for capturing discrete arches, individual avalanches, tap release, afterflow grains, and zero-dose increments.

**4.2 SPH and Material Point Method (MPM)**

No published precedent was identified for SPH or MPM applied specifically to screw feeders or auger powder dosing. While these methods handle large deformation, free surfaces, and elasto-plastic constitutive laws without mesh distortion, the resolution needed near a small outlet erodes their speed advantage, and stochastic particle-scale stoppages remain unresolved.

### 5. Analytical and Reduced-Order Feed-Factor Models

Several reduced-order approaches predict screw-feeder mass flow without particle-level resolution. The basic analytical model treats mass flow as the product of screw conveying volume, powder density, and rotational speed: ṁ = φ·A·P·ρ·ω·C, where φ is the loading coefficient, A is cross-sectional area, P is pitch, ρ is bulk density, ω is speed, and C is an inclination correction (pqac-00000024). Bascone et al. (2020) developed a hybrid mechanistic-empirical model combining hopper stress, pressure-dependent powder densification, vortex-related volumetric efficiency, and first-order-plus-dead-time (FOPDT) dynamics: ṁ_level = nPAρ_e(t)η (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022). Fathollahi et al. (2020) introduced a "displacement-feed factor" concept where feed rate equals effective displacement density multiplied by displaced volume per unit time, capturing how powder density evolves during feeding through densification, dilation, and elastic recovery (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000028). These models evaluate in milliseconds and are ideal for closed-loop control and Bayesian sampling, though they cannot uniquely identify microscopic cohesion or friction parameters.

### 6. Speed-Up Techniques

Three principal speed-up strategies have been documented for DEM of screw feeders:

1. **Coarse-graining**: Original particles of radius R are replaced with larger particles of radius R′ = S_f·R, with interaction laws adjusted to preserve gravitational potential-energy density, kinetic-energy density, and dissipation. Particle count decreases by S_f³ while total mass is conserved. The method produced acceptable agreement for angle of repose but cannot reproduce exact heap shape (pqac-00000029).

2. **Reduced stiffness/Young's modulus**: McBride and Cleary used stiffness values of 250–1000 N/m (far below physical values) to enable larger time steps, achieving average overlaps of only 0.15–0.17% (pqac-00000006). This is the most common approach for making DEM tractable.

3. **GPU acceleration**: Available in modern commercial codes (Rocky, EDEM) and some research implementations. Quantitative speed-ups for micro-auger applications were not reported in the retrieved literature, but GPU DEM can reduce wall time by 10–100× depending on particle count and hardware.

### 7. Calibration and Inverse Inference

**7.1 Current Practice**

The dominant calibration approach uses design of experiments (DoE) combined with multivariate regression or response surface methods. El-Kassem et al. (2021) used a D-optimal quadratic design varying six DEM parameters across three levels, requiring 40–53 simulation runs per study (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000018). Meier et al. (2018) calibrated surface energy by deterministically matching simulated and experimental angle-of-repose values (pqac-00000019). General DEM literature references Bayesian optimization and Bayesian filtering for parameter calibration, but no feeder-specific Bayesian inference from dosing data was identified in the retrieved record.

**7.2 Opportunity for Simulation-Based Bayesian Calibration**

The "dosing fingerprint" concept—mass per revolution versus tilt and speed, tap-released mass, afterflow time constant, and no-flow fraction—provides a rich, multi-output dataset well suited for simulation-based inference. A practical workflow would train a Gaussian-process or neural-network emulator on a Latin-hypercube DEM design, then use the emulator in approximate Bayesian computation (ABC) or neural posterior estimation to obtain posterior distributions over cohesion, friction, and rolling resistance. The reduced-order feed-factor model could serve as the discrepancy or mean-function layer.

### 8. Connection to Powder-Bed Additive Manufacturing Spreadability

DEM has been extensively applied to simulate powder spreading in powder-bed fusion using LIGGGHTS and other codes (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000033). Cohesive energy density has been identified as a particularly influential DEM parameter for spreading; if cohesion is omitted, simulations overestimate particle mobility and fail to capture actual powder-bed characteristics (pqac-00000032). Spreadability is closely related to flowability, integrating particle-size distribution, morphology, density, surface texture, and cohesion. However, standard flowability tests (Hall/Carney flow, angle of repose, shear cell) do not fully reproduce the constrained geometry of layer deposition and should be treated as indicators rather than direct predictors of spreading performance (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000034). The same DEM parameters calibrated from auger dosing data—particularly cohesion, friction, and rolling resistance—can be transferred directly to powder-spreading simulations to anticipate spreadability.

### 9. Comparison Table of Simulation Methods

The following table provides a detailed comparison of all identified methods, codes, models, and validation approaches:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

### 10. Published DEM Input Parameters

Concrete published parameter values that can serve as starting points for calibration:

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

### 11. Suitability Ranking for Millimetre-Scale Auger Dosing

The methods are ranked by their suitability for modeling a millimetre-scale auger dispensing cohesive fine powders (10–100 µm) and salts:

<artifact id="artifact-02"/>

### 12. Key Findings and Recommendations

1. **DEM with cohesion is the gold standard** for this application. The existing LIGGGHTS model with Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, and EPSD2 rolling friction already reproduces the 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters, providing an unusually strong validation anchor.

2. **No published study has used simulation-based Bayesian calibration to infer powder properties from feeder/dosing data.** This represents a clear research gap. Current calibration relies on DoE + regression or deterministic angle-of-repose matching (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000019).

3. **Coarse-graining is the primary speed-up strategy** for reducing the 26–30 CPU-min/rev cost, but care is needed: coarse particles must remain small relative to the 3 mm outlet to preserve arching and intermittency statistics (pqac-00000029).

4. **Analytical feed-factor models** provide an essential fast companion for real-time control and Bayesian sampling. The hybrid mechanistic-empirical FOPDT model of Bascone et al. (2020) combines screw geometry, pressure-dependent densification, vortex efficiency, and dynamics (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022).

5. **For AM spreadability prediction**, the same DEM cohesion and friction parameters calibrated from dosing data can be transferred to powder-spreading simulations. Effective surface energy of ~0.1 mJ/m² for Ti-6Al-4V (pqac-00000016) and cohesion energy density of 30–70 kJ/m³ for cohesive lactose (pqac-00000018) provide transferable prior ranges.

6. **Continuum methods (Eulerian CFD, SPH, MPM) are not recommended** as primary models for this application due to insufficient resolution at the 3 mm outlet scale and inability to resolve stochastic dose-to-dose events.

7. **Coupled CFD-DEM** should be reserved as an escalation model only when dry DEM leaves systematic residuals correlated with speed, powder permeability, or air displacement effects."}
