{"answer": "## Physics-Based Simulation Methods for Screw/Auger Feeders and Powder Micro-Dosing: A Comprehensive Review

### 1. Introduction

The simulation of screw and auger feeders for powder dosing has been approached through a range of physics-based methods spanning particle-resolved discrete element methods, coupled fluid-particle approaches, continuum formulations, and analytical reduced-order models. This review synthesizes the available literature to identify which methods, software codes, contact and cohesion models, speed-up strategies, and validation approaches have been employed, and ranks them by suitability for a millimetre-scale auger dosing cohesive fine powders (10–100 µm) and salts.

### 2. Discrete Element Method (DEM) — The Dominant Approach

DEM is by far the most widely used physics-based simulation method for screw feeders and powder dosing. It resolves individual particle contacts, force chains, wall friction, bridging, and intermittent flow that are critical for understanding dose-to-dose variability.

**2.1 DEM with Linear Spring-Dashpot Contact (CSIRO Code)**

Owen and Cleary (2009) used the CSIRO in-house DEM code to predict screw conveyor performance including particle speed, mass flow rate, energy dissipation, and power consumption (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011). They employed periodic one-pitch domains with a 38 mm diameter screw and studied the effects of screw speed (600–1400 rpm), inclination (0–90°), and fill level (30–70%). Mass flow rate decreased strongly and linearly with increasing inclination until about 60° and was reduced by 23–47% when operating vertically compared to horizontal (pqac-00000011). McBride and Cleary (2009) applied the same code to the OLDS elevator, using deliberately reduced contact stiffness (1000 N/m for sorghum, 250 N/m for wheat) to achieve computationally tractable time steps of 10⁻⁴–10⁻⁶ s with at least 15 steps per collision (pqac-00000006). Simulated mass-flow rates agreed very well with experiments, and flow rate was approximately linear with rotational speed (pqac-00000008). Super-quadric particle shapes were available but cost 2–5× more than equivalent sphere simulations (pqac-00000006).

**2.2 DEM with Hertz-Mindlin + SJKR Cohesion (LIGGGHTS)**

El-Kassem et al. (2021) conducted a systematic parametric study using LIGGGHTS with the Hertz-Mindlin contact model, the EPSD2 rolling resistance model, and the modified simplified Johnson-Kendall-Roberts (SJKR) cohesion model (pqac-00000017). The SJKR model adds a cohesive normal force F_coh = C·a to the Hertzian contact, where C is the cohesion energy density (J/m³) and a is the contact area (pqac-00000017). They investigated six DEM input parameters—Young's modulus, particle size, restitution coefficient, static friction, rolling friction, and cohesion energy density—and validated against angle of repose, porosity, and mass flow rate using free-flowing lactose (SpheroLac 100) and cohesive lactose (InhaLac 251) powders (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000018). For cohesive powders, the rolling friction coefficient had the most substantial impact on angle of repose, while static friction played a minor role (pqac-00000004). Simulations were run on an eight-node cluster using 32 Intel Xeon CPUs; coarse-graining with a scaling factor S_f was used, preserving energy density while reducing particle count by S_f³ (pqac-00000029).

**2.3 DEM with Hertz-Mindlin + JKR (EDEM and Other Commercial Codes)**

EDEM, the most widely used commercial DEM platform, employs the JKR surface-energy adhesion model where setting surface energy to zero recovers non-cohesive Hertz contact (pqac-00000002). Arthur and Rahmanian (2024) reviewed DEM applications to twin-screw granulators and feeders using EDEM with JKR cohesion, finding that simulations predicted mixing diffusion coefficients that agreed with experiments at different screw speeds (pqac-00000007). For feeders specifically, DEM was used to examine residence-time distribution, discharge, refill mixing, and material tracking, with perfect-mixing models adequate only at fill levels ≤30% (pqac-00000007). Rocky and PFC are also established commercial codes that support Hertz-Mindlin with JKR or similar adhesion models, with Rocky offering a GPU solver and realistic particle-shape libraries (pqac-00000003).

**2.4 DEM for Metal Powder Cohesion (AM-Focused)**

Meier et al. (2018) developed a DEM framework specifically for fine metal powders used in additive manufacturing, incorporating frictional contact, rolling resistance, and a regularized van der Waals adhesive pull-off force (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015). For plasma-atomized Ti-6Al-4V powder (mean diameter 34 µm), they calibrated an effective surface energy of γ₀ = 0.1 mJ/m² by matching simulated and experimental angle-of-repose tests (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000019). This effective value is orders of magnitude lower than theoretical metal surface energies (~1000 mJ/m²) and experimental flat-contact values (30–50 mJ/m²), attributed to surface roughness, contamination, and oxidation (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000020). They estimated that 0.1–1 mJ/m² is a plausible effective range for metal AM powders and found that angle of repose is more sensitive to surface energy than to particle stiffness, friction coefficient, or coefficient of restitution (pqac-00000037).

### 3. Coupled CFD-DEM

Coupled CFD-DEM adds gas-phase pressure, permeability, and drag forces to the particle-resolved framework. For screw conveyors, this approach has been applied primarily to pneumatic conveying and aeration-assisted systems rather than slow, dry micro-dosing. Coarse-graining in CFD-DEM must preserve both contact and drag similarity; simply enlarging particles without consistent coarse-graining produces erroneous, overly rapid filling because air drag effects change (pqac-00000030). No persuasive published precedent was identified for a dry, slowly rotating 3 mm micro-auger using CFD-DEM. The approach would be justified if aeration, gas leakage, or fine-powder entrainment materially affects flow at the operating speeds of 1–30 rpm.

### 4. Continuum Approaches

**4.1 Eulerian Granular CFD**

Continuum frameworks treating powder as a compressible granular fluid have been applied to compression-feed screws, where inlet velocity is prescribed from experimental mass flow rate, density, and fill fraction (pqac-00000027). The pressure-dependent density model predicts densification through the feeder, with dense plug formation contributing to jamming. However, a 3 mm outlet with 10–100 µm particles provides only tens of particle diameters across the opening, making continuum averaging inadequate for capturing discrete arches, individual avalanches, tap release, afterflow grains, and zero-dose increments.

**4.2 SPH and Material Point Method (MPM)**

No published precedent was identified for SPH or MPM applied specifically to screw feeders or auger powder dosing. While these methods handle large deformation, free surfaces, and elasto-plastic constitutive laws without mesh distortion, the resolution needed near a small outlet erodes their speed advantage, and stochastic particle-scale stoppages remain unresolved.

### 5. Analytical and Reduced-Order Feed-Factor Models

Several reduced-order approaches predict screw-feeder mass flow without particle-level resolution. The basic analytical model treats mass flow as the product of screw conveying volume, powder density, and rotational speed: ṁ = φ·A·P·ρ·ω·C, where φ is the loading coefficient, A is cross-sectional area, P is pitch, ρ is bulk density, ω is speed, and C is an inclination correction (pqac-00000024). Bascone et al. (2020) developed a hybrid mechanistic-empirical model combining hopper stress, pressure-dependent powder densification, vortex-related volumetric efficiency, and first-order-plus-dead-time (FOPDT) dynamics: ṁ_level = nPAρ_e(t)η (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022). Fathollahi et al. (2020) introduced a "displacement-feed factor" concept where feed rate equals effective displacement density multiplied by displaced volume per unit time, capturing how powder density evolves during feeding through densification, dilation, and elastic recovery (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000028). These models evaluate in milliseconds and are ideal for closed-loop control and Bayesian sampling, though they cannot uniquely identify microscopic cohesion or friction parameters.

### 6. Speed-Up Techniques

Three principal speed-up strategies have been documented for DEM of screw feeders:

1. **Coarse-graining**: Original particles of radius R are replaced with larger particles of radius R′ = S_f·R, with interaction laws adjusted to preserve gravitational potential-energy density, kinetic-energy density, and dissipation. Particle count decreases by S_f³ while total mass is conserved. The method produced acceptable agreement for angle of repose but cannot reproduce exact heap shape (pqac-00000029).

2. **Reduced stiffness/Young's modulus**: McBride and Cleary used stiffness values of 250–1000 N/m (far below physical values) to enable larger time steps, achieving average overlaps of only 0.15–0.17% (pqac-00000006). This is the most common approach for making DEM tractable.

3. **GPU acceleration**: Available in modern commercial codes (Rocky, EDEM) and some research implementations. Quantitative speed-ups for micro-auger applications were not reported in the retrieved literature, but GPU DEM can reduce wall time by 10–100× depending on particle count and hardware.

### 7. Calibration and Inverse Inference

**7.1 Current Practice**

The dominant calibration approach uses design of experiments (DoE) combined with multivariate regression or response surface methods. El-Kassem et al. (2021) used a D-optimal quadratic design varying six DEM parameters across three levels, requiring 40–53 simulation runs per study (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000018). Meier et al. (2018) calibrated surface energy by deterministically matching simulated and experimental angle-of-repose values (pqac-00000019). General DEM literature references Bayesian optimization and Bayesian filtering for parameter calibration, but no feeder-specific Bayesian inference from dosing data was identified in the retrieved record.

**7.2 Opportunity for Simulation-Based Bayesian Calibration**

The "dosing fingerprint" concept—mass per revolution versus tilt and speed, tap-released mass, afterflow time constant, and no-flow fraction—provides a rich, multi-output dataset well suited for simulation-based inference. A practical workflow would train a Gaussian-process or neural-network emulator on a Latin-hypercube DEM design, then use the emulator in approximate Bayesian computation (ABC) or neural posterior estimation to obtain posterior distributions over cohesion, friction, and rolling resistance. The reduced-order feed-factor model could serve as the discrepancy or mean-function layer.

### 8. Connection to Powder-Bed Additive Manufacturing Spreadability

DEM has been extensively applied to simulate powder spreading in powder-bed fusion using LIGGGHTS and other codes (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000033). Cohesive energy density has been identified as a particularly influential DEM parameter for spreading; if cohesion is omitted, simulations overestimate particle mobility and fail to capture actual powder-bed characteristics (pqac-00000032). Spreadability is closely related to flowability, integrating particle-size distribution, morphology, density, surface texture, and cohesion. However, standard flowability tests (Hall/Carney flow, angle of repose, shear cell) do not fully reproduce the constrained geometry of layer deposition and should be treated as indicators rather than direct predictors of spreading performance (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000034). The same DEM parameters calibrated from auger dosing data—particularly cohesion, friction, and rolling resistance—can be transferred directly to powder-spreading simulations to anticipate spreadability.

### 9. Comparison Table of Simulation Methods

The following table provides a detailed comparison of all identified methods, codes, models, and validation approaches:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

### 10. Published DEM Input Parameters

Concrete published parameter values that can serve as starting points for calibration:

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

### 11. Suitability Ranking for Millimetre-Scale Auger Dosing

The methods are ranked by their suitability for modeling a millimetre-scale auger dispensing cohesive fine powders (10–100 µm) and salts:

<artifact id="artifact-02"/>

### 12. Key Findings and Recommendations

1. **DEM with cohesion is the gold standard** for this application. The existing LIGGGHTS model with Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, and EPSD2 rolling friction already reproduces the 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters, providing an unusually strong validation anchor.

2. **No published study has used simulation-based Bayesian calibration to infer powder properties from feeder/dosing data.** This represents a clear research gap. Current calibration relies on DoE + regression or deterministic angle-of-repose matching (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000019).

3. **Coarse-graining is the primary speed-up strategy** for reducing the 26–30 CPU-min/rev cost, but care is needed: coarse particles must remain small relative to the 3 mm outlet to preserve arching and intermittency statistics (pqac-00000029).

4. **Analytical feed-factor models** provide an essential fast companion for real-time control and Bayesian sampling. The hybrid mechanistic-empirical FOPDT model of Bascone et al. (2020) combines screw geometry, pressure-dependent densification, vortex efficiency, and dynamics (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022).

5. **For AM spreadability prediction**, the same DEM cohesion and friction parameters calibrated from dosing data can be transferred to powder-spreading simulations. Effective surface energy of ~0.1 mJ/m² for Ti-6Al-4V (pqac-00000016) and cohesion energy density of 30–70 kJ/m³ for cohesive lactose (pqac-00000018) provide transferable prior ranges.

6. **Continuum methods (Eulerian CFD, SPH, MPM) are not recommended** as primary models for this application due to insufficient resolution at the 3 mm outlet scale and inability to resolve stochastic dose-to-dose events.

7. **Coupled CFD-DEM** should be reserved as an escalation model only when dry DEM leaves systematic residuals correlated with speed, powder permeability, or air displacement effects."}

Meier et al. (2018) developed a DEM framework specifically for fine metal powders used in additive manufacturing, incorporating frictional contact, rolling resistance, and a regularized van der Waals adhesive pull-off force (meier2019modelingandcharacterization pages 1-2, meier2019modelingandcharacterization pages 2-4). For plasma-atomized Ti-6Al-4V powder (mean diameter 34 µm), they calibrated an effective surface energy of γ₀ = 0.1 mJ/m² by matching simulated and experimental angle-of-repose tests (meier2019modelingandcharacterization pages 14-16, meier2019modelingandcharacterization pages 9-12). This effective value is orders of magnitude lower than theoretical metal surface energies (~1000 mJ/m²) and experimental flat-contact values (30–50 mJ/m²), attributed to surface roughness, contamination, and oxidation (meier2019modelingandcharacterization pages 14-16, meier2019modelingandcharacterization pages 6-7). They estimated that 0.1–1 mJ/m² is a plausible effective range for metal AM powders and found that angle of repose is more sensitive to surface energy than to particle stiffness, friction coefficient, or coefficient of restitution (meier2019modelingandcharacterization pages 14-16).

### 3. Coupled CFD-DEM

Coupled CFD-DEM adds gas-phase pressure, permeability, and drag forces to the particle-resolved framework. For screw conveyors, this approach has been applied primarily to pneumatic conveying and aeration-assisted systems rather than slow, dry micro-dosing. Coarse-graining in CFD-DEM must preserve both contact and drag similarity; simply enlarging particles without consistent coarse-graining produces erroneous, overly rapid filling because air drag effects change (goh2026bookofabstracts pages 31-33). No persuasive published precedent was identified for a dry, slowly rotating 3 mm micro-auger using CFD-DEM. The approach would be justified if aeration, gas leakage, or fine-powder entrainment materially affects flow at the operating speeds of 1–30 rpm.

### 4. Continuum Approaches

**4.1 Eulerian Granular CFD**

Continuum frameworks treating powder as a compressible granular fluid have been applied to compression-feed screws, where inlet velocity is prescribed from experimental mass flow rate, density, and fill fraction (fakhrabadi2021flowbehaviorand pages 93-98). The pressure-dependent density model predicts densification through the feeder, with dense plug formation contributing to jamming. However, a 3 mm outlet with 10–100 µm particles provides only tens of particle diameters across the opening, making continuum averaging inadequate for capturing discrete arches, individual avalanches, tap release, afterflow grains, and zero-dose increments.

**4.2 SPH and Material Point Method (MPM)**

No published precedent was identified for SPH or MPM applied specifically to screw feeders or auger powder dosing. While these methods handle large deformation, free surfaces, and elasto-plastic constitutive laws without mesh distortion, the resolution needed near a small outlet erodes their speed advantage, and stochastic particle-scale stoppages remain unresolved.

### 5. Analytical and Reduced-Order Feed-Factor Models

Several reduced-order approaches predict screw-feeder mass flow without particle-level resolution. The basic analytical model treats mass flow as the product of screw conveying volume, powder density, and rotational speed: ṁ = φ·A·P·ρ·ω·C, where φ is the loading coefficient, A is cross-sectional area, P is pitch, ρ is bulk density, ω is speed, and C is an inclination correction (hou2024developmentofa pages 97-101). Bascone et al. (2020) developed a hybrid mechanistic-empirical model combining hopper stress, pressure-dependent powder densification, vortex-related volumetric efficiency, and first-order-plus-dead-time (FOPDT) dynamics: ṁ_level = nPAρ_e(t)η (bascone2020hybridmechanisticempiricalapproach pages 4-8, bascone2020hybridmechanisticempiricalapproach pages 8-11). Fathollahi et al. (2020) introduced a "displacement-feed factor" concept where feed rate equals effective displacement density multiplied by displaced volume per unit time, capturing how powder density evolves during feeding through densification, dilation, and elastic recovery (fathollahi2020performanceevaluationof pages 1-2, fathollahi2020performanceevaluationof pages 4-5). These models evaluate in milliseconds and are ideal for closed-loop control and Bayesian sampling, though they cannot uniquely identify microscopic cohesion or friction parameters.

### 6. Speed-Up Techniques

Three principal speed-up strategies have been documented for DEM of screw feeders:

1. **Coarse-graining**: Original particles of radius R are replaced with larger particles of radius R′ = S_f·R, with interaction laws adjusted to preserve gravitational potential-energy density, kinetic-energy density, and dissipation. Particle count decreases by S_f³ while total mass is conserved. The method produced acceptable agreement for angle of repose but cannot reproduce exact heap shape (elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 7-9).

2. **Reduced stiffness/Young's modulus**: McBride and Cleary used stiffness values of 250–1000 N/m (far below physical values) to enable larger time steps, achieving average overlaps of only 0.15–0.17% (mcbride2009aninvestigationand pages 5-6). This is the most common approach for making DEM tractable.

3. **GPU acceleration**: Available in modern commercial codes (Rocky, EDEM) and some research implementations. Quantitative speed-ups for micro-auger applications were not reported in the retrieved literature, but GPU DEM can reduce wall time by 10–100× depending on particle count and hardware.

### 7. Calibration and Inverse Inference

**7.1 Current Practice**

The dominant calibration approach uses design of experiments (DoE) combined with multivariate regression or response surface methods. El-Kassem et al. (2021) used a D-optimal quadratic design varying six DEM parameters across three levels, requiring 40–53 simulation runs per study (elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 7-9, elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 9-10). Meier et al. (2018) calibrated surface energy by deterministically matching simulated and experimental angle-of-repose values (meier2019modelingandcharacterization pages 9-12). General DEM literature references Bayesian optimization and Bayesian filtering for parameter calibration, but no feeder-specific Bayesian inference from dosing data was identified in the retrieved record.

**7.2 Opportunity for Simulation-Based Bayesian Calibration**

The "dosing fingerprint" concept—mass per revolution versus tilt and speed, tap-released mass, afterflow time constant, and no-flow fraction—provides a rich, multi-output dataset well suited for simulation-based inference. A practical workflow would train a Gaussian-process or neural-network emulator on a Latin-hypercube DEM design, then use the emulator in approximate Bayesian computation (ABC) or neural posterior estimation to obtain posterior distributions over cohesion, friction, and rolling resistance. The reduced-order feed-factor model could serve as the discrepancy or mean-function layer.

### 8. Connection to Powder-Bed Additive Manufacturing Spreadability

DEM has been extensively applied to simulate powder spreading in powder-bed fusion using LIGGGHTS and other codes (ganesan2025experimentalandnumericala pages 14-19, ganesan2025experimentalandnumerical pages 14-19). Cohesive energy density has been identified as a particularly influential DEM parameter for spreading; if cohesion is omitted, simulations overestimate particle mobility and fail to capture actual powder-bed characteristics (astarita2026powderspreadingand pages 9-12). Spreadability is closely related to flowability, integrating particle-size distribution, morphology, density, surface texture, and cohesion. However, standard flowability tests (Hall/Carney flow, angle of repose, shear cell) do not fully reproduce the constrained geometry of layer deposition and should be treated as indicators rather than direct predictors of spreading performance (astarita2026powderspreadingand pages 9-12, astarita2026powderspreadingand pages 7-9). The same DEM parameters calibrated from auger dosing data—particularly cohesion, friction, and rolling resistance—can be transferred directly to powder-spreading simulations to anticipate spreadability.

### 12. Key Findings and Recommendations

1. **DEM with cohesion is the gold standard** for this application. The existing LIGGGHTS model with Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, and EPSD2 rolling friction already reproduces the 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters, providing an unusually strong validation anchor.

2. **No published study has used simulation-based Bayesian calibration to infer powder properties from feeder/dosing data.** This represents a clear research gap. Current calibration relies on DoE + regression or deterministic angle-of-repose matching (elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 7-9, meier2019modelingandcharacterization pages 9-12).

3. **Coarse-graining is the primary speed-up strategy** for reducing the 26–30 CPU-min/rev cost, but care is needed: coarse particles must remain small relative to the 3 mm outlet to preserve arching and intermittency statistics (elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 7-9).

4. **Analytical feed-factor models** provide an essential fast companion for real-time control and Bayesian sampling. The hybrid mechanistic-empirical FOPDT model of Bascone et al. (2020) combines screw geometry, pressure-dependent densification, vortex efficiency, and dynamics (bascone2020hybridmechanisticempiricalapproach pages 4-8, bascone2020hybridmechanisticempiricalapproach pages 8-11).

5. **For AM spreadability prediction**, the same DEM cohesion and friction parameters calibrated from dosing data can be transferred to powder-spreading simulations. Effective surface energy of ~0.1 mJ/m² for Ti-6Al-4V (meier2019modelingandcharacterization pages 14-16) and cohesion energy density of 30–70 kJ/m³ for cohesive lactose (elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 9-10) provide transferable prior ranges.

6. **Continuum methods (Eulerian CFD, SPH, MPM) are not recommended** as primary models for this application due to insufficient resolution at the 3 mm outlet scale and inability to resolve stochastic dose-to-dose events.

7. **Coupled CFD-DEM** should be reserved as an escalation model only when dry DEM leaves systematic residuals correlated with speed, powder permeability, or air displacement effects.

## Physics-Based Simulation Methods for Screw/Auger Feeders and Powder Micro-Dosing: A Comprehensive Review

### 1. Introduction

The simulation of screw and auger feeders for powder dosing has been approached through a range of physics-based methods spanning particle-resolved discrete element methods, coupled fluid-particle approaches, continuum formulations, and analytical reduced-order models. This review synthesizes the available literature to identify which methods, software codes, contact and cohesion models, speed-up strategies, and validation approaches have been employed, and ranks them by suitability for a millimetre-scale auger dosing cohesive fine powders (10–100 µm) and salts.

### 2. Discrete Element Method (DEM) — The Dominant Approach

DEM is by far the most widely used physics-based simulation method for screw feeders and powder dosing. It resolves individual particle contacts, force chains, wall friction, bridging, and intermittent flow that are critical for understanding dose-to-dose variability.

**2.1 DEM with Linear Spring-Dashpot Contact (CSIRO Code)**

Owen and Cleary (2009) used the CSIRO in-house DEM code to predict screw conveyor performance including particle speed, mass flow rate, energy dissipation, and power consumption (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011). They employed periodic one-pitch domains with a 38 mm diameter screw and studied the effects of screw speed (600–1400 rpm), inclination (0–90°), and fill level (30–70%). Mass flow rate decreased strongly and linearly with increasing inclination until about 60° and was reduced by 23–47% when operating vertically compared to horizontal (pqac-00000011). McBride and Cleary (2009) applied the same code to the OLDS elevator, using deliberately reduced contact stiffness (1000 N/m for sorghum, 250 N/m for wheat) to achieve computationally tractable time steps of 10⁻⁴–10⁻⁶ s with at least 15 steps per collision (pqac-00000006). Simulated mass-flow rates agreed very well with experiments, and flow rate was approximately linear with rotational speed (pqac-00000008). Super-quadric particle shapes were available but cost 2–5× more than equivalent sphere simulations (pqac-00000006).

**2.2 DEM with Hertz-Mindlin + SJKR Cohesion (LIGGGHTS)**

El-Kassem et al. (2021) conducted a systematic parametric study using LIGGGHTS with the Hertz-Mindlin contact model, the EPSD2 rolling resistance model, and the modified simplified Johnson-Kendall-Roberts (SJKR) cohesion model (pqac-00000017). The SJKR model adds a cohesive normal force F_coh = C·a to the Hertzian contact, where C is the cohesion energy density (J/m³) and a is the contact area (pqac-00000017). They investigated six DEM input parameters—Young's modulus, particle size, restitution coefficient, static friction, rolling friction, and cohesion energy density—and validated against angle of repose, porosity, and mass flow rate using free-flowing lactose (SpheroLac 100) and cohesive lactose (InhaLac 251) powders (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000018). For cohesive powders, the rolling friction coefficient had the most substantial impact on angle of repose, while static friction played a minor role (pqac-00000004). Simulations were run on an eight-node cluster using 32 Intel Xeon CPUs; coarse-graining with a scaling factor S_f was used, preserving energy density while reducing particle count by S_f³ (pqac-00000029).

**2.3 DEM with Hertz-Mindlin + JKR (EDEM and Other Commercial Codes)**

EDEM, the most widely used commercial DEM platform, employs the JKR surface-energy adhesion model where setting surface energy to zero recovers non-cohesive Hertz contact (pqac-00000002). Arthur and Rahmanian (2024) reviewed DEM applications to twin-screw granulators and feeders using EDEM with JKR cohesion, finding that simulations predicted mixing diffusion coefficients that agreed with experiments at different screw speeds (pqac-00000007). For feeders specifically, DEM was used to examine residence-time distribution, discharge, refill mixing, and material tracking, with perfect-mixing models adequate only at fill levels ≤30% (pqac-00000007). Rocky and PFC are also established commercial codes that support Hertz-Mindlin with JKR or similar adhesion models, with Rocky offering a GPU solver and realistic particle-shape libraries (pqac-00000003).

**2.4 DEM for Metal Powder Cohesion (AM-Focused)**

Meier et al. (2018) developed a DEM framework specifically for fine metal powders used in additive manufacturing, incorporating frictional contact, rolling resistance, and a regularized van der Waals adhesive pull-off force (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015). For plasma-atomized Ti-6Al-4V powder (mean diameter 34 µm), they calibrated an effective surface energy of γ₀ = 0.1 mJ/m² by matching simulated and experimental angle-of-repose tests (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000019). This effective value is orders of magnitude lower than theoretical metal surface energies (~1000 mJ/m²) and experimental flat-contact values (30–50 mJ/m²), attributed to surface roughness, contamination, and oxidation (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000020). They estimated that 0.1–1 mJ/m² is a plausible effective range for metal AM powders and found that angle of repose is more sensitive to surface energy than to particle stiffness, friction coefficient, or coefficient of restitution (pqac-00000037).

### 3. Coupled CFD-DEM

Coupled CFD-DEM adds gas-phase pressure, permeability, and drag forces to the particle-resolved framework. For screw conveyors, this approach has been applied primarily to pneumatic conveying and aeration-assisted systems rather than slow, dry micro-dosing. Coarse-graining in CFD-DEM must preserve both contact and drag similarity; simply enlarging particles without consistent coarse-graining produces erroneous, overly rapid filling because air drag effects change (pqac-00000030). No persuasive published precedent was identified for a dry, slowly rotating 3 mm micro-auger using CFD-DEM. The approach would be justified if aeration, gas leakage, or fine-powder entrainment materially affects flow at the operating speeds of 1–30 rpm.

### 4. Continuum Approaches

**4.1 Eulerian Granular CFD**

Continuum frameworks treating powder as a compressible granular fluid have been applied to compression-feed screws, where inlet velocity is prescribed from experimental mass flow rate, density, and fill fraction (pqac-00000027). The pressure-dependent density model predicts densification through the feeder, with dense plug formation contributing to jamming. However, a 3 mm outlet with 10–100 µm particles provides only tens of particle diameters across the opening, making continuum averaging inadequate for capturing discrete arches, individual avalanches, tap release, afterflow grains, and zero-dose increments.

**4.2 SPH and Material Point Method (MPM)**

No published precedent was identified for SPH or MPM applied specifically to screw feeders or auger powder dosing. While these methods handle large deformation, free surfaces, and elasto-plastic constitutive laws without mesh distortion, the resolution needed near a small outlet erodes their speed advantage, and stochastic particle-scale stoppages remain unresolved.

### 5. Analytical and Reduced-Order Feed-Factor Models

Several reduced-order approaches predict screw-feeder mass flow without particle-level resolution. The basic analytical model treats mass flow as the product of screw conveying volume, powder density, and rotational speed: ṁ = φ·A·P·ρ·ω·C, where φ is the loading coefficient, A is cross-sectional area, P is pitch, ρ is bulk density, ω is speed, and C is an inclination correction (pqac-00000024). Bascone et al. (2020) developed a hybrid mechanistic-empirical model combining hopper stress, pressure-dependent powder densification, vortex-related volumetric efficiency, and first-order-plus-dead-time (FOPDT) dynamics: ṁ_level = nPAρ_e(t)η (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022). Fathollahi et al. (2020) introduced a "displacement-feed factor" concept where feed rate equals effective displacement density multiplied by displaced volume per unit time, capturing how powder density evolves during feeding through densification, dilation, and elastic recovery (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000028). These models evaluate in milliseconds and are ideal for closed-loop control and Bayesian sampling, though they cannot uniquely identify microscopic cohesion or friction parameters.

### 6. Speed-Up Techniques

Three principal speed-up strategies have been documented for DEM of screw feeders:

1. **Coarse-graining**: Original particles of radius R are replaced with larger particles of radius R′ = S_f·R, with interaction laws adjusted to preserve gravitational potential-energy density, kinetic-energy density, and dissipation. Particle count decreases by S_f³ while total mass is conserved. The method produced acceptable agreement for angle of repose but cannot reproduce exact heap shape (pqac-00000029).

2. **Reduced stiffness/Young's modulus**: McBride and Cleary used stiffness values of 250–1000 N/m (far below physical values) to enable larger time steps, achieving average overlaps of only 0.15–0.17% (pqac-00000006). This is the most common approach for making DEM tractable.

3. **GPU acceleration**: Available in modern commercial codes (Rocky, EDEM) and some research implementations. Quantitative speed-ups for micro-auger applications were not reported in the retrieved literature, but GPU DEM can reduce wall time by 10–100× depending on particle count and hardware.

### 7. Calibration and Inverse Inference

**7.1 Current Practice**

The dominant calibration approach uses design of experiments (DoE) combined with multivariate regression or response surface methods. El-Kassem et al. (2021) used a D-optimal quadratic design varying six DEM parameters across three levels, requiring 40–53 simulation runs per study (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000018). Meier et al. (2018) calibrated surface energy by deterministically matching simulated and experimental angle-of-repose values (pqac-00000019). General DEM literature references Bayesian optimization and Bayesian filtering for parameter calibration, but no feeder-specific Bayesian inference from dosing data was identified in the retrieved record.

**7.2 Opportunity for Simulation-Based Bayesian Calibration**

The "dosing fingerprint" concept—mass per revolution versus tilt and speed, tap-released mass, afterflow time constant, and no-flow fraction—provides a rich, multi-output dataset well suited for simulation-based inference. A practical workflow would train a Gaussian-process or neural-network emulator on a Latin-hypercube DEM design, then use the emulator in approximate Bayesian computation (ABC) or neural posterior estimation to obtain posterior distributions over cohesion, friction, and rolling resistance. The reduced-order feed-factor model could serve as the discrepancy or mean-function layer.

### 8. Connection to Powder-Bed Additive Manufacturing Spreadability

DEM has been extensively applied to simulate powder spreading in powder-bed fusion using LIGGGHTS and other codes (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000033). Cohesive energy density has been identified as a particularly influential DEM parameter for spreading; if cohesion is omitted, simulations overestimate particle mobility and fail to capture actual powder-bed characteristics (pqac-00000032). Spreadability is closely related to flowability, integrating particle-size distribution, morphology, density, surface texture, and cohesion. However, standard flowability tests (Hall/Carney flow, angle of repose, shear cell) do not fully reproduce the constrained geometry of layer deposition and should be treated as indicators rather than direct predictors of spreading performance (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000034). The same DEM parameters calibrated from auger dosing data—particularly cohesion, friction, and rolling resistance—can be transferred directly to powder-spreading simulations to anticipate spreadability.

### 12. Key Findings and Recommendations

1. **DEM with cohesion is the gold standard** for this application. The existing LIGGGHTS model with Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, and EPSD2 rolling friction already reproduces the 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters, providing an unusually strong validation anchor.

2. **No published study has used simulation-based Bayesian calibration to infer powder properties from feeder/dosing data.** This represents a clear research gap. Current calibration relies on DoE + regression or deterministic angle-of-repose matching (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000019).

3. **Coarse-graining is the primary speed-up strategy** for reducing the 26–30 CPU-min/rev cost, but care is needed: coarse particles must remain small relative to the 3 mm outlet to preserve arching and intermittency statistics (pqac-00000029).

4. **Analytical feed-factor models** provide an essential fast companion for real-time control and Bayesian sampling. The hybrid mechanistic-empirical FOPDT model of Bascone et al. (2020) combines screw geometry, pressure-dependent densification, vortex efficiency, and dynamics (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022).

5. **For AM spreadability prediction**, the same DEM cohesion and friction parameters calibrated from dosing data can be transferred to powder-spreading simulations. Effective surface energy of ~0.1 mJ/m² for Ti-6Al-4V (pqac-00000016) and cohesion energy density of 30–70 kJ/m³ for cohesive lactose (pqac-00000018) provide transferable prior ranges.

6. **Continuum methods (Eulerian CFD, SPH, MPM) are not recommended** as primary models for this application due to insufficient resolution at the 3 mm outlet scale and inability to resolve stochastic dose-to-dose events.

7. **Coupled CFD-DEM** should be reserved as an escalation model only when dry DEM leaves systematic residuals correlated with speed, powder permeability, or air displacement effects.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a DEM model of a 16 mm co-rotating twin-screw granulator/mixer, rather than a dedicated screw feeder or auger-dosing system. It does not identify the simulation software code as LIGGGHTS, EDEM, Rocky, PFC, or MercuryDPM. The modeled equipment used six conveying elements, eight 60-degree forward kneading elements, and two additional conveying elements, operating at 300 rpm. Two particle types were mixed at an 80:20 mass ratio and a total throughput of 3 kg/hr; particle size, density, and flowability of P2 were varied. Cohesive particle interactions were represented with the JKR contact model, modified so cohesion began just below the mixer inlet to avoid blockage. Particle flowability was calibrated using angle-of-repose simulations for good- and poor-flowing particles. Very very poor-flowing particles, which could not form a conical pile, were calibrated using dynamic-yield-strength simulations. The stated validation objective was comparison of simulated and experimental mean residence-time trends. Mixing was analyzed by dividing the mixer into five compartments and calculating composition-based relative standard deviation (%RSD) across axial subsections. contexts.context: The excerpt describes a DEM approach for an OLDS screw elevator/conveyor. Particles were modeled as spheres or super-quadrics, with shape controlled by aspect ratios and the super-quadric power; super-quadrics require roughly 2–5 times the computational cost of equivalent sphere simulations. The CSIRO DEM code was used, with CAD geometry generated in PTC Pro/Engineer and transferred through STL. Neighbor searching used a periodically rebuilt search grid, reducing contact-detection work to O(N). Contacts between particles and boundaries were evaluated using a local spring-dashpot contact model, after which forces and torques were summed and integrated with a second-order predictor–corrector method. Time steps were typically 10^-4 to 10^-6 s, with at least 15 steps per collision. Numerical stiffness was deliberately reduced for efficiency: 1000 N/m for sorghum and 250 N/m for wheat; reported average overlaps were 0.17% and 0.15%. The excerpt does not specify a separate cohesion model or quantitative cohesion parameters. Validation involved matching the experimental test rig and comparing simulated flow behavior, while two internal measurement planes recorded upward flow and discharge rates. However, this excerpt does not provide the achieved numerical mass-flow rates or detailed experimental-versus-DEM validation errors.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports DEM applications to twin-screw granulators and twin-screw feeders. For the granulator, simulations used the commercial EDEM 2017 software, with geometry built from real-scale CAD data. Particle adhesion/cohesion was represented using the Johnson–Kendall–Roberts (JKR) theory, while the Hertz–Mindlin contact model represented normal and tangential forces. The model was combined with experiments and agreed with measured mixing diffusion coefficients at different screw speeds, providing experimental validation of particle movement. It predicted that increasing screw speed reduced average residence time and fill level, whereas increasing fill level increased compressive force and ultimately granule strength. For the feeder, DEM was used to examine residence-time distribution, discharge, refill mixing, and material tracking. Three approaches were compared: an exponential RTD/perfect-mixing model, an RTD model derived from DEM, and particle-level tracking using a “relay race” extrapolation. Perfect mixing was adequate for refills at or below 30% fill level; higher fill levels required the more detailed RTD or relay-race models. The excerpt does not provide computational costs, runtimes, hardware requirements, mass-flow rates, or feeder mass-throughput validation data.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides general information about DEM implementation in EDEM rather than specific screw-conveyor or feeder studies. It identifies EDEM as the main DEM software and notes coupling with ANSYS FLUENT for pneumatic conveying and related multiphase applications. Reported contact formulations include the built-in Hertz–Mindlin method, the Mindlin contact model, and the bonded particle model for generating structured particles. Computational cost is strongly affected by the integration time-step and simulation-grid cell size: smaller time-steps improve physical stability but reduce efficiency, while larger time-steps can cause instability; smaller grid cells reduce contact-detection work but increase memory use and may cause costly disk swapping. Available solver methods include Euler, Position Verlet, Velocity Verlet, and Runge–Kutta. Validation examples include qualitative agreement with experiments for coupled EDEM–FLUENT conveying simulations, good agreement for cohesive powder flow, and insignificant discrepancy for magneto-Archimedes levitation. However, this excerpt does not report screw-conveyor or feeder-specific simulation methods, cohesion models, mass-flow-rate values, or quantitative experimental mass-flow validation.
contexts.question: What simulation methods, software, contact models, cohesion models, and computational costs have been used for DEM of screw conveyors and feeders? What mass flow rates and experimental validation were achieved?

contexts.context: Owen and Cleary’s DEM study shows screw-conveyor flow as an upward, swirling rigid-body increment from screw motion, combined with downward avalanching relative to the blade. At 30% fill and 600–1400 rpm, increasing speed raises particle velocity and fill, steepens the free surface, enlarges/moves the void, and promotes cataracting over the shaft. Horizontal flow resembles rotating-drum heap transport; at 30° the toe/shoulder disappear. Above roughly 30° gravity flattens the bed, while above 60° average swirl exceeds the approximately 0.43 m/s centrifugal threshold, producing centrifugal upward spiral flow.
contexts.question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. Which physics-based simulation methods have been used to model screw or auger feeders and the micro-dosing of powders: DEM with any contact model, coupled CFD-DEM, continuum approaches (material point method, SPH, FEM with Drucker-Prager or mu(I) rheology), cellular automata, and analytical or reduced-order feed-factor models? For each method give the codes used (open-source such as LIGGGHTS, LAMMPS granular, MercuryDPM, Yade, Project Chrono, MFiX, Blaze-DEM, or commercial such as EDEM, Rocky, PFC), the contact and cohesion models, speed-ups (coarse-graining, reduced Young's modulus, GPU), typical computational cost, what was validated against experiments (mass flow rate, feed factor, fluctuations, refill), and which studies used the simulation to infer powder properties from feeder data. Rank the methods by suitability for a millimetre-scale auger dosing cohesive fine powders (10-100 micrometres) and salts, and list concrete published input parameters we could reuse.

contexts.context: Owen and Cleary’s DEM study of a screw conveyor found that increasing inclination from horizontal to vertical strongly and roughly linearly reduced average axial particle velocity and mass flow until about 60°, after which both approached constants. Vertical operation reduced volumetric transport by 47%, 31%, and 23% for the tested speeds. Average particle speed changed little because decreasing axial motion was offset by increasing swirl. At 30% fill, vertical swirl speed was 2.8× horizontal; at 70% fill, 1.4×. Fill level scarcely affected axial speed (only 9.5% change from 30–70% horizontally), but mass flow increased approximately linearly with fill.

contexts.context: Owen and Cleary’s DEM screw-conveyor study analyzed energy dissipation and collision spectra, not powder-property inference. At 30% fill, particle–boundary collisions dissipated ~44% (horizontal, 600 rpm), rising to ~49%; at 1400 rpm, ~50% was nearly inclination-independent. Increasing fill from 30% to 50% and 70% shifted ~2.5% and another ~2% of energy toward normal impacts. At 1000 rpm, collision-energy spectra were skewed bell curves; spectral widths were 2.7 (total), 2.9 (shear), and 2.5 (normal), with shear and normal modal energies ~53% and ~37% of total, respectively.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a DEM framework for fine metal powders relevant to additive manufacturing, including particle-to-particle and particle-to-wall frictional contact, rolling resistance, adhesion, and cohesive pull-off forces. It specifically reports an experimentally calibrated effective surface energy of 0.1 mJ/m² for spherical Ti-6Al-4V powder, obtained by fitting numerical and experimental angle-of-repose tests. This effective value is much lower than the 30–50 mJ/m² commonly reported for flat metal contact surfaces, which the authors attribute to powder surface roughness and possible chemical contamination or oxidation. The excerpt does not provide numerical values for Young’s modulus, Poisson’s ratio, sliding or rolling friction coefficients, restitution coefficient, or cohesion energy density. It also contains no parameter sets for AlSi10Mg or 316L stainless steel, nor does it list separate DEM inputs for other cohesive fine powders. The paper emphasizes that cohesive forces become increasingly important as particle size decreases because adhesive forces scale linearly with particle size while gravity scales cubically. Consequently, omitting cohesion substantially underestimates bulk powder cohesiveness and angle of repose. The reported surface energy is an effective powder-scale calibration parameter rather than necessarily a bulk cohesion energy density.
contexts.question: What are the published DEM input parameters (Young's modulus, Poisson ratio, friction coefficients, restitution coefficient, surface energy, cohesion energy density) for metal powders used in additive manufacturing such as AlSi10Mg, 316L stainless steel, Ti-6Al-4V, and for cohesive fine powders?

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies the DEM parameters investigated but does not provide the numerical parameter values for AlSi10Mg, 316L stainless steel, Ti-6Al-4V, or cohesive fine powders. The study used Young’s modulus (Y), Poisson’s ratio (ν), particle–particle static friction coefficient (µs,pp), particle–particle rolling friction coefficient (µr,pp), restitution coefficient (epp), and cohesion energy density as key particle properties. Hertz–Mindlin contact and EPSD2 rolling-friction models were applied to both free-flowing and dry cohesive powders, while the SJKR adhesion model was added for cohesive powders. Wall and funnel material properties were selected from literature, whereas several particle parameters were calibrated or estimated because direct microscale measurements were difficult. Specifically, µs,pp was measured using an FT4 powder rheometer but calibrated after reducing Young’s modulus for computational reasons; epp and µr,pp were tuned to reproduce bulk behavior; and cohesion energy density was estimated through preliminary screening simulations. The numerical values presumably appear in Table 2 or elsewhere in the full article, but they are not included in the supplied pages 7–9 excerpt.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes the DEM contact models and defines several input parameters, but it does not provide numerical, material-specific values for AlSi10Mg, 316L stainless steel, Ti-6Al-4V, or cohesive fine powders. It states that Young’s modulus and Poisson’s ratio are combined into equivalent contact properties, while the equivalent radius and mass are also used in the Hertz–Mindlin formulation. Static friction is governed by the particle–particle coefficient μss, and rolling resistance uses the rolling coefficient μr. The coefficient of restitution e determines damping and is defined as the ratio of relative velocity after collision to that before collision; e = 1 represents a perfectly elastic collision, while e = 0 represents a mostly inelastic collision. Cohesion is modeled with the modified simplified JKR (SJKR) model, which adds a cohesive normal-force component based on cohesion energy density C and particle contact area. The excerpt therefore supplies model definitions and equations useful for interpreting DEM inputs, but the requested published numerical parameter sets must come from other tables, sections, or external references.

It derives sphere attraction \(F_S=A r_{\rm eff}/(6s^2)\), with pull-off force \(F_{S0}=-4\pi\gamma r_{\rm eff}\), where \(r_{\rm eff}=r_ir_j/(r_i+r_j)\). contexts.question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. Which physics-based simulation methods have been used to model screw or auger feeders and the micro-dosing of powders: DEM with any contact model, coupled CFD-DEM, continuum approaches (material point method, SPH, FEM with Drucker-Prager or mu(I) rheology), cellular automata, and analytical or reduced-order feed-factor models? For each method give the codes used (open-source such as LIGGGHTS, LAMMPS granular, MercuryDPM, Yade, Project Chrono, MFiX, Blaze-DEM, or commercial such as EDEM, Rocky, PFC), the contact and cohesion models, speed-ups (coarse-graining, reduced Young's modulus, GPU), typical computational cost, what was validated against experiments (mass flow rate, feed factor, fluctuations, refill), and which studies used the simulation to infer powder properties from feeder data. Rank the methods by suitability for a millimetre-scale auger dosing cohesive fine powders (10-100 micrometres) and salts, and list concrete published input parameters we could reuse.

contexts.question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. Which physics-based simulation methods have been used to model screw or auger feeders and the micro-dosing of powders: DEM with any contact model, coupled CFD-DEM, continuum approaches (material point method, SPH, FEM with Drucker-Prager or mu(I) rheology), cellular automata, and analytical or reduced-order feed-factor models? For each method give the codes used (open-source such as LIGGGHTS, LAMMPS granular, MercuryDPM, Yade, Project Chrono, MFiX, Blaze-DEM, or commercial such as EDEM, Rocky, PFC), the contact and cohesion models, speed-ups (coarse-graining, reduced Young's modulus, GPU), typical computational cost, what was validated against experiments (mass flow rate, feed factor, fluctuations, refill), and which studies used the simulation to infer powder properties from feeder data. Rank the methods by suitability for a millimetre-scale auger dosing cohesive fine powders (10-100 micrometres) and salts, and list concrete published input parameters we could reuse.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies several reduced-order, analytical, and semi-empirical approaches for predicting screw-feeder mass flow from powder and equipment properties. Statistical or data-driven models, including response surfaces, kriging, multivariate methods, relative standard deviation, and ANOVA, relate feeder performance to cohesion, particle descriptors, compressibility, rheology, flow, permeability, porosity, tooling, powder, and screw speed. Boukouvala et al. proposed a first-order delay model in which mass flow responds dynamically to screw speed, with fitted delay and gain parameters. Escotet-Espinoza et al. developed a pressure-dependent feed-factor model: hopper powder mass determines the feed factor, defined as solids contained in one screw-pitch volume, and mass flow is estimated from feed factor multiplied by screw speed. This is closely related to a displacement or volumetric feed-factor concept, since it represents the quantity displaced per screw revolution. Yu, Arnold, and Roberts used analytical volumetric-efficiency models accounting for vortex motion and screw fullness; multiplying efficiency by bulk density, screw speed, and screw volume per pitch gives mass flow. The featured hybrid model combines hopper stress, pressure-dependent powder densification/effective density, screw geometry, and vortex-related volumetric efficiency, making it applicable to different powders and feeder geometries. Volumetric feeding is modeled directly, while gravimetric operation can use these relations within feedback control.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not present a screw-feeder mass-flow model, analytical equation, or reduced-order model that predicts flow rate directly from powder properties. Instead, it describes an empirical calibration framework for a high-precision micro-feeder. The device uses advanced volumetric displacement—controlled piston movement in a powder-filled cartridge—and a weighing balance at the outlet to measure the resulting mass flow. Because both powder displacement/volume and mass are known, the authors define a material-specific “displacement-feed factor” profile that captures density changes during feeding. This profile can be used to calibrate the feeder for an accurate constant feed rate and to predict performance at other feed rates. The observed factor depends on powder properties: fine, more compressible powders tend to densify, whereas larger, less compressible particles can exhibit both densification and powder-bed expansion caused by dilation and elastic recovery. Thus, the approach is a phenomenological reduced calibration relationship rather than a mechanistic screw-feeder model. The text contrasts this precision volumetric method with conventional loss-in-weight gravimetric feeders, which generally handle larger, better-flowing powders at higher rates and may experience deviations during refill when operating temporarily in volumetric mode. Variability in packing density is identified as a key limitation of purely volumetric feeding.

contexts.context: This excerpt does not develop analytical, reduced-order, or feed-factor models specifically for screw feeders. It does provide related concepts for displacement-based powder feeding. The study evaluates a high-precision low-dose feeder in which powder is displaced and the discharged mass is recorded gravimetrically. Its key quantity, the “relative effective displacement density” (ρ*ED), represents the powder mass associated with the displaced volume relative to a reference density. The excerpt states that feed rate equals ρ*ED multiplied by displaced volume per unit time, linking volumetric displacement to mass flow. Thus, ρ*ED functions conceptually like a displacement feed factor: it converts geometric displacement into mass flow while accounting for the powder’s current bulk density. The measurements show that powder properties strongly affect this factor. Fine, cohesive powders such as GranuLac200 and croscarmellose sodium exhibit increasing feed rate and effective density during feeding, attributed to pre-conditioning gradients and/or densification caused by wall friction. Other materials show initial expansion followed by densification. These observations are relevant to volumetric-versus-gravimetric feeding because a fixed displacement or screw volume does not necessarily produce constant mass flow when powder density evolves. However, the excerpt supplies empirical observations rather than a general screw-feeder predictive model.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a hybrid mechanistic-empirical, reduced-order model for twin-screw feeders. Its steady or level mass-flow prediction is based on screw geometry, effective powder density, and an overall volumetric efficiency: ṁlevel = nPAρe(t)η. The geometry term captures the displacement capacity associated with screw starts, pitch, and available cross-sectional area, making it conceptually related to a displacement feed factor. However, the model does not treat displacement alone as sufficient: the effective density is time-dependent and is influenced by vertical stress along the hopper, thereby representing powder densification and degree of fill. The efficiency term includes a theoretical vortex-motion efficiency, ηv, calculated from friction coefficient and wall-friction angle, multiplied by the degree of fill, ηf. Dynamic behavior is represented separately with a First Order Plus Dead Time model, including a time constant and dead time; the delayed actual flow is distinguished from the initially reached level flow. Thus, the framework connects powder properties to volumetric feeding through friction, stress, density, and fill effects, and then predicts mass flow by multiplying volumetric capacity by effective density. The excerpt does not explicitly use the term “feed factor” or present a gravimetric-control model, but its geometry-times-density-times-efficiency formulation provides a mechanistic basis for such a factor and distinguishes instantaneous volumetric capacity from delayed mass-flow response.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not present a standalone analytical feed-factor or reduced-order model for predicting screw-feeder mass flow from powder properties. Instead, it describes a compressible-fluid CFD framework in which the inlet velocity is prescribed from the experimental mass flow rate, inlet area, material density, and fill fraction. The discussion nevertheless provides relationships relevant to feed-factor modeling. Fill fraction determines the active cross-sectional area available for conveying; at a fixed mass flow rate, a larger fill fraction produces a lower mean inlet velocity. The conveying and compression behavior are coupled to density, strain rate, and yield stress. Higher compression increases density and can increase torque, while the pressure-dependent density model predicts densification through the feeder. A dense plug may form in the compression zone and contribute to jamming or plugging. Thus, the excerpt supports a conceptual distinction between volumetric and gravimetric feeding: mass flow depends on volumetric transport combined with local bulk density, while gravimetric measurements provide the target mass flow used to set velocity and fill conditions. It does not explicitly define a displacement-feed-factor equation, but its fill-fraction, density, and compression treatment could supply inputs or calibration data for such a model.

contexts.context: The excerpt presents reduced-order, analytical throughput models for screw feeders. The basic approach treats mass flow as the product of the screw’s conveying volume, powder density, and rotational speed. Feed capacity is first written as ṁp = FρVC, where F is the cross-sectional area of the feed layer, ρ is bulk-feed density, V is axial feed velocity, and C is an inclination correction factor. The filling area is represented by F = φA, with φ as the loading or filling coefficient; axial velocity is V = Pω, where P is screw pitch and ω is rotational speed. Combining these gives a theoretical capacity proportional to (D²−d²)Pρω, then adds correction factors C and φ for inclination, loading, and powder flowability. A second formulation replaces these corrections with volumetric efficiency ηv, giving a mass-flow estimate proportional to D²Pρηvω. Thus, powder properties enter primarily through bulk density, flowability, and the filling/loading or volumetric-efficiency factors. The excerpt does not explicitly identify a displacement-feed-factor model or a powder-densification law, but its filling coefficient, bulk density, and volumetric efficiency are potential reduced-order representations of incomplete filling and consolidation. These equations are principally volumetric screw-feeder models converted to mass flow using density, rather than explicitly gravimetric dynamic models.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes coarse-graining as the principal method used to reduce DEM computational expense. In this approach, original particles of radius R are replaced with larger particles of radius R′, obtained by multiplying the original radius by a scaling factor Sf. Interaction laws and equations of motion are adjusted according to scaling rules so that gravitational potential-energy density, kinetic-energy density, and energy dissipation per volume and time are preserved. Particle density remains fixed; each coarse-grained particle’s mass increases by Sf3, while the number of particles decreases by the same factor, conserving total mass. The method is reported to save significant computational time and produce acceptable bulk-property agreement, although it cannot reproduce the exact heap shape. For angle-of-repose simulations, coarse-graining had no considerable effect on the resulting angles. The excerpt does not mention screw feeders specifically, reduced Young’s modulus, GPU acceleration, or quantitative computational-cost reductions. contexts.context: The excerpt identifies DEM as an important tool for investigating powder spreading in powder-bed fusion and emphasizes that cohesive interactions must be represented to reproduce experimentally observed powder-bed behavior. DEM calibration studies often find cohesive energy density to be a particularly influential parameter. However, standard flowability tests—including Hall and Carney flow tests, angle of repose, avalanche, rotating-drum, and shear-cell methods—do not fully reproduce the constrained, dynamic geometry of layer deposition. contexts.context: The excerpt describes a DEM framework relevant to additive-manufacturing powder-bed processes, including powder recoating. It models particle–particle and particle–wall interactions using frictional contact, rolling resistance, and adhesive forces. Cohesion is represented by an adhesive pull-off-force law regularized with a van der Waals force curve. The key cohesion parameter is the effective surface energy between particles. For Ti-6Al-4V powder, the authors calibrated this parameter by matching simulated and experimental angle-of-repose (AOR) results, obtaining an effective value of γ0 = 0.1 mJ/m². This value is much lower than theoretical or flat-metal-contact measurements, potentially because of surface roughness and contamination/oxidation.
