Question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. Which physics-based simulation methods have been used to model screw or auger feeders and the micro-dosing of powders: DEM with any contact model, coupled CFD-DEM, continuum approaches (material point method, SPH, FEM with Drucker-Prager or mu(I) rheology), cellular automata, and analytical or reduced-order feed-factor models? For each method give the codes used (open-source such as LIGGGHTS, LAMMPS granular, MercuryDPM, Yade, Project Chrono, MFiX, Blaze-DEM, or commercial such as EDEM, Rocky, PFC), the contact and cohesion models, speed-ups (coarse-graining, reduced Young's modulus, GPU), typical computational cost, what was validated against experiments (mass flow rate, feed factor, fluctuations, refill), and which studies used the simulation to infer powder properties from feeder data. Rank the methods by suitability for a millimetre-scale auger dosing cohesive fine powders (10-100 micrometres) and salts, and list concrete published input parameters we could reuse.

## Physics-Based Simulation Methods for Screw/Auger Feeders and Powder Micro-Dosing: A Comprehensive Review

### 1. Introduction

The simulation of screw and auger feeders for powder dosing has been approached through a range of physics-based methods spanning particle-resolved discrete element methods, coupled fluid-particle approaches, continuum formulations, and analytical reduced-order models. This review synthesizes the available literature to identify which methods, software codes, contact and cohesion models, speed-up strategies, and validation approaches have been employed, and ranks them by suitability for a millimetre-scale auger dosing cohesive fine powders (10–100 µm) and salts.

### 2. Discrete Element Method (DEM) — The Dominant Approach

DEM is by far the most widely used physics-based simulation method for screw feeders and powder dosing. It resolves individual particle contacts, force chains, wall friction, bridging, and intermittent flow that are critical for understanding dose-to-dose variability.

**2.1 DEM with Linear Spring-Dashpot Contact (CSIRO Code)**

Owen and Cleary (2009) used the CSIRO in-house DEM code to predict screw conveyor performance including particle speed, mass flow rate, energy dissipation, and power consumption (owen2009predictionofscrew pages 1-2, owen2009predictionofscrew pages 4-8, owen2009predictionofscrew pages 10-11). They employed periodic one-pitch domains with a 38 mm diameter screw and studied the effects of screw speed (600–1400 rpm), inclination (0–90°), and fill level (30–70%). Mass flow rate decreased strongly and linearly with increasing inclination until about 60° and was reduced by 23–47% when operating vertically compared to horizontal (owen2009predictionofscrew pages 10-11). McBride and Cleary (2009) applied the same code to the OLDS elevator, using deliberately reduced contact stiffness (1000 N/m for sorghum, 250 N/m for wheat) to achieve computationally tractable time steps of 10⁻⁴–10⁻⁶ s with at least 15 steps per collision (mcbride2009aninvestigationand pages 5-6). Simulated mass-flow rates agreed very well with experiments, and flow rate was approximately linear with rotational speed (mcbride2009aninvestigationand pages 18-19). Super-quadric particle shapes were available but cost 2–5× more than equivalent sphere simulations (mcbride2009aninvestigationand pages 5-6).

**2.2 DEM with Hertz-Mindlin + SJKR Cohesion (LIGGGHTS)**

El-Kassem et al. (2021) conducted a systematic parametric study using LIGGGHTS with the Hertz-Mindlin contact model, the EPSD2 rolling resistance model, and the modified simplified Johnson-Kendall-Roberts (SJKR) cohesion model (elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 5-6). The SJKR model adds a cohesive normal force F_coh = C·a to the Hertzian contact, where C is the cohesion energy density (J/m³) and a is the contact area (elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 5-6). They investigated six DEM input parameters—Young's modulus, particle size, restitution coefficient, static friction, rolling friction, and cohesion energy density—and validated against angle of repose, porosity, and mass flow rate using free-flowing lactose (SpheroLac 100) and cohesive lactose (InhaLac 251) powders (elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 7-9, elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 9-10). For cohesive powders, the rolling friction coefficient had the most substantial impact on angle of repose, while static friction played a minor role (elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 23-24). Simulations were run on an eight-node cluster using 32 Intel Xeon CPUs; coarse-graining with a scaling factor S_f was used, preserving energy density while reducing particle count by S_f³ (elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 7-9).

**2.3 DEM with Hertz-Mindlin + JKR (EDEM and Other Commercial Codes)**

EDEM, the most widely used commercial DEM platform, employs the JKR surface-energy adhesion model where setting surface energy to zero recovers non-cohesive Hertz contact (karkala2021analysisofpowder pages 19-24). Arthur and Rahmanian (2024) reviewed DEM applications to twin-screw granulators and feeders using EDEM with JKR cohesion, finding that simulations predicted mixing diffusion coefficients that agreed with experiments at different screw speeds (arthur2024processsimulationof pages 17-18). For feeders specifically, DEM was used to examine residence-time distribution, discharge, refill mixing, and material tracking, with perfect-mixing models adequate only at fill levels ≤30% (arthur2024processsimulationof pages 17-18). Rocky and PFC are also established commercial codes that support Hertz-Mindlin with JKR or similar adhesion models, with Rocky offering a GPU solver and realistic particle-shape libraries (fourie2019discreteelementsimulation pages 18-21).

**2.4 DEM for Metal Powder Cohesion (AM-Focused)**

Meier et al. (2018) developed a DEM framework specifically for fine metal powders used in additive manufacturing, incorporating frictional contact, rolling resistance, and a regularized van der Waals adhesive pull-off force (meier2019modelingandcharacterization pages 1-2, meier2019modelingandcharacterization pages 2-4). For plasma-atomized Ti-6Al-4V powder (mean diameter 34 µm), they calibrated an effective surface energy of γ₀ = 0.1 mJ/m² by matching simulated and experimental angle-of-repose tests (meier2019modelingandcharacterization pages 14-16, meier2019modelingandcharacterization pages 9-12). This effective value is orders of magnitude lower than theoretical metal surface energies (~1000 mJ/m²) and experimental flat-contact values (30–50 mJ/m²), attributed to surface roughness, contamination, and oxidation (meier2019modelingandcharacterization pages 14-16, meier2019modelingandcharacterization pages 6-7). They estimated that 0.1–1 mJ/m² is a plausible effective range for metal AM powders and found that angle of repose is more sensitive to surface energy than to particle stiffness, friction coefficient, or coefficient of restitution (meier2019modelingandcharacterization pages 14-16).

### 3. Coupled CFD-DEM

Coupled CFD-DEM adds gas-phase pressure, permeability, and drag forces to the particle-resolved framework. For screw conveyors, this approach has been applied primarily to pneumatic conveying and aeration-assisted systems rather than slow, dry micro-dosing. Coarse-graining in CFD-DEM must preserve both contact and drag similarity; simply enlarging particles without consistent coarse-graining produces erroneous, overly rapid filling because air drag effects change (goh2026bookofabstracts pages 31-33). No persuasive published precedent was identified for a dry, slowly rotating 3 mm micro-auger using CFD-DEM. The approach would be justified if aeration, gas leakage, or fine-powder entrainment materially affects flow at the operating speeds of 1–30 rpm.

### 4. Continuum Approaches

**4.1 Eulerian Granular CFD**

Continuum frameworks treating powder as a compressible granular fluid have been applied to compression-feed screws, where inlet velocity is prescribed from experimental mass flow rate, density, and fill fraction (fakhrabadi2021flowbehaviorand pages 93-98). The pressure-dependent density model predicts densification through the feeder, with dense plug formation contributing to jamming. However, a 3 mm outlet with 10–100 µm particles provides only tens of particle diameters across the opening, making continuum averaging inadequate for capturing discrete arches, individual avalanches, tap release, afterflow grains, and zero-dose increments.

**4.2 SPH and Material Point Method (MPM)**

No published precedent was identified for SPH or MPM applied specifically to screw feeders or auger powder dosing. While these methods handle large deformation, free surfaces, and elasto-plastic constitutive laws without mesh distortion, the resolution needed near a small outlet erodes their speed advantage, and stochastic particle-scale stoppages remain unresolved.

### 5. Analytical and Reduced-Order Feed-Factor Models

Several reduced-order approaches predict screw-feeder mass flow without particle-level resolution. The basic analytical model treats mass flow as the product of screw conveying volume, powder density, and rotational speed: ṁ = φ·A·P·ρ·ω·C, where φ is the loading coefficient, A is cross-sectional area, P is pitch, ρ is bulk density, ω is speed, and C is an inclination correction (hou2024developmentofa pages 97-101). Bascone et al. (2020) developed a hybrid mechanistic-empirical model combining hopper stress, pressure-dependent powder densification, vortex-related volumetric efficiency, and first-order-plus-dead-time (FOPDT) dynamics: ṁ_level = nPAρ_e(t)η (bascone2020hybridmechanisticempiricalapproach pages 4-8, bascone2020hybridmechanisticempiricalapproach pages 8-11). Fathollahi et al. (2020) introduced a "displacement-feed factor" concept where feed rate equals effective displacement density multiplied by displaced volume per unit time, capturing how powder density evolves during feeding through densification, dilation, and elastic recovery (fathollahi2020performanceevaluationof pages 1-2, fathollahi2020performanceevaluationof pages 4-5). These models evaluate in milliseconds and are ideal for closed-loop control and Bayesian sampling, though they cannot uniquely identify microscopic cohesion or friction parameters.

### 6. Speed-Up Techniques

Three principal speed-up strategies have been documented for DEM of screw feeders:

1. **Coarse-graining**: Original particles of radius R are replaced with larger particles of radius R′ = S_f·R, with interaction laws adjusted to preserve gravitational potential-energy density, kinetic-energy density, and dissipation. Particle count decreases by S_f³ while total mass is conserved. The method produced acceptable agreement for angle of repose but cannot reproduce exact heap shape (elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 7-9).

2. **Reduced stiffness/Young's modulus**: McBride and Cleary used stiffness values of 250–1000 N/m (far below physical values) to enable larger time steps, achieving average overlaps of only 0.15–0.17% (mcbride2009aninvestigationand pages 5-6). This is the most common approach for making DEM tractable.

3. **GPU acceleration**: Available in modern commercial codes (Rocky, EDEM) and some research implementations. Quantitative speed-ups for micro-auger applications were not reported in the retrieved literature, but GPU DEM can reduce wall time by 10–100× depending on particle count and hardware.

### 7. Calibration and Inverse Inference

**7.1 Current Practice**

The dominant calibration approach uses design of experiments (DoE) combined with multivariate regression or response surface methods. El-Kassem et al. (2021) used a D-optimal quadratic design varying six DEM parameters across three levels, requiring 40–53 simulation runs per study (elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 7-9, elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 9-10). Meier et al. (2018) calibrated surface energy by deterministically matching simulated and experimental angle-of-repose values (meier2019modelingandcharacterization pages 9-12). General DEM literature references Bayesian optimization and Bayesian filtering for parameter calibration, but no feeder-specific Bayesian inference from dosing data was identified in the retrieved record.

**7.2 Opportunity for Simulation-Based Bayesian Calibration**

The "dosing fingerprint" concept—mass per revolution versus tilt and speed, tap-released mass, afterflow time constant, and no-flow fraction—provides a rich, multi-output dataset well suited for simulation-based inference. A practical workflow would train a Gaussian-process or neural-network emulator on a Latin-hypercube DEM design, then use the emulator in approximate Bayesian computation (ABC) or neural posterior estimation to obtain posterior distributions over cohesion, friction, and rolling resistance. The reduced-order feed-factor model could serve as the discrepancy or mean-function layer.

### 8. Connection to Powder-Bed Additive Manufacturing Spreadability

DEM has been extensively applied to simulate powder spreading in powder-bed fusion using LIGGGHTS and other codes (ganesan2025experimentalandnumericala pages 14-19, ganesan2025experimentalandnumerical pages 14-19). Cohesive energy density has been identified as a particularly influential DEM parameter for spreading; if cohesion is omitted, simulations overestimate particle mobility and fail to capture actual powder-bed characteristics (astarita2026powderspreadingand pages 9-12). Spreadability is closely related to flowability, integrating particle-size distribution, morphology, density, surface texture, and cohesion. However, standard flowability tests (Hall/Carney flow, angle of repose, shear cell) do not fully reproduce the constrained geometry of layer deposition and should be treated as indicators rather than direct predictors of spreading performance (astarita2026powderspreadingand pages 9-12, astarita2026powderspreadingand pages 7-9). The same DEM parameters calibrated from auger dosing data—particularly cohesion, friction, and rolling resistance—can be transferred directly to powder-spreading simulations to anticipate spreadability.

### 12. Key Findings and Recommendations

1. **DEM with cohesion is the gold standard** for this application. The existing LIGGGHTS model with Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, and EPSD2 rolling friction already reproduces the 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters, providing an unusually strong validation anchor.

2. **No published study has used simulation-based Bayesian calibration to infer powder properties from feeder/dosing data.** This represents a clear research gap. Current calibration relies on DoE + regression or deterministic angle-of-repose matching (elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 7-9, meier2019modelingandcharacterization pages 9-12).

3. **Coarse-graining is the primary speed-up strategy** for reducing the 26–30 CPU-min/rev cost, but care is needed: coarse particles must remain small relative to the 3 mm outlet to preserve arching and intermittency statistics (elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 7-9).

4. **Analytical feed-factor models** provide an essential fast companion for real-time control and Bayesian sampling. The hybrid mechanistic-empirical FOPDT model of Bascone et al. (2020) combines screw geometry, pressure-dependent densification, vortex efficiency, and dynamics (bascone2020hybridmechanisticempiricalapproach pages 4-8, bascone2020hybridmechanisticempiricalapproach pages 8-11).

5. **For AM spreadability prediction**, the same DEM cohesion and friction parameters calibrated from dosing data can be transferred to powder-spreading simulations. Effective surface energy of ~0.1 mJ/m² for Ti-6Al-4V (meier2019modelingandcharacterization pages 14-16) and cohesion energy density of 30–70 kJ/m³ for cohesive lactose (elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 9-10) provide transferable prior ranges.

6. **Continuum methods (Eulerian CFD, SPH, MPM) are not recommended** as primary models for this application due to insufficient resolution at the 3 mm outlet scale and inability to resolve stochastic dose-to-dose events.

7. **Coupled CFD-DEM** should be reserved as an escalation model only when dry DEM leaves systematic residuals correlated with speed, powder permeability, or air displacement effects.

| Method | Software / code | Contact / cohesion model | Speed-ups used | Typical computational cost | Validated against experiments | Studies using inverse inference from feeder data |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| DEM: Hertz–Mindlin + SJKR | **LIGGGHTS**; applicable also in LAMMPS-derived granular implementations | Hertz–Mindlin normal/tangential contact; Coulomb sliding; modified simplified JKR force, `F_coh = C·A_contact`; EPSD2 rolling resistance. Published cohesive-powder screening used cohesion-energy density `C_pp = 30–70 kJ m⁻³` (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018) | Reduced Young’s modulus; coarse-graining with particle radius scaled by `S_f`, particle mass by `S_f³`, and count reduced correspondingly; domain trimming; MPI parallelism. Coarse-graining preserved angle of repose reasonably but not exact heap geometry (pqac-00000029) | Strongly particle-count and stiffness dependent. The user’s millimetre auger requires **26–30 CPU-min per revolution**; published powder calibration campaigns require tens of full runs (40 noncohesive; 53 cohesive) on multicore hardware (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000029) | Angle of repose, porosity, mass-flow rate and bulk density in powder-calibration studies; screw studies commonly target throughput, inclination/speed response, torque and power. AOR is most often used for cohesion/friction calibration rather than feeder output (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000013) | **No published feeder-data Bayesian inversion identified.** El-Kassem et al. used design of experiments and multivariate regression, not Bayesian inference; parameters were calibrated to bulk AOR/porosity/flow responses (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000018) |
| DEM: linear spring–dashpot | **CSIRO in-house DEM code** used by Cleary, Owen and McBride | Linear normal and tangential spring–dashpot contact with friction; spheres or superquadrics; no explicit cohesion in the cited screw-conveyor studies (pqac-00000006) | Periodic one-pitch domains; `O(N)` grid neighbour search; deliberately reduced stiffness (`250 N m⁻¹` for wheat; `1000 N m⁻¹` for sorghum); spheres instead of superquadrics. Superquadrics cost about 2–5× more than spheres (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006) | Explicit time steps typically `10⁻⁴–10⁻⁶ s`, with at least 15 steps per collision. Runtime was not reported; periodic single-pitch models substantially reduce particle count (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006) | Screw-conveyor mass flow, particle axial/swirl velocity, inclination and fill-level effects, power and energy dissipation; OLDS-elevator mass-flow predictions agreed very well with experiments. Vertical operation reduced volumetric transport by 23–47% relative to horizontal operation in one study (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000011) | **None identified.** These studies were forward prediction and engineering optimization, not inference of powder properties from feeder measurements |
| DEM: Hertz–Mindlin + JKR | **EDEM** (commercial) | Hertz–Mindlin normal/tangential contact; Mindlin–Deresiewicz tangential response; Coulomb friction; rolling resistance; JKR surface-energy adhesion. Setting surface energy to zero recovers noncohesive Hertz contact (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000007) | Reduced modulus/stiffness, simplified spherical particles, limited geometry and prescribed inlet throughput are common; GPU acceleration is available in modern EDEM, but quantitative speed-up was not reported in the cited feeder/granulator studies | Usually hours to days for realistic twin-screw equipment; exact runtimes were not reported. Cost rises sharply for true 10–100 μm PSDs and for refill simulations requiring long residence times | Twin-screw mixing diffusion coefficient, mean residence-time trends, fill level, refill mixing and residence-time distribution; feeder studies examined discharge and refill, with perfect-mixing approximations adequate only at ≤30% fill in the cited analysis (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000007) | **No feeder-based Bayesian inference identified.** Published work calibrates JKR surface energy or friction to AOR/dynamic-yield-strength tests and then validates residence-time or mixing behavior (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002) |
| DEM: Hertz–Mindlin + JKR or adhesive pull-off law | **Rocky, PFC, MercuryDPM, Yade, Project Chrono, Blaze-DEM**, and research codes; direct screw-feeder evidence is strongest for EDEM and in-house codes, while the others are established DEM options rather than well-documented micro-auger precedents (pqac-00000003) | Hertz–Mindlin with JKR; alternatively regularized van der Waals/pull-off force plus sliding friction and rolling resistance. For 34 μm Ti-6Al-4V, effective surface energy `γ = 0.1 mJ m⁻²`; a useful metal-powder prior is approximately `0.1–1 mJ m⁻²` (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000037) | GPU solvers in Rocky, Chrono and Blaze-DEM; reduced modulus; periodic sectors; sphere or multisphere approximations; coarse-graining. Shape-resolved particles improve interlocking but increase cost | GPU DEM can reduce wall time substantially, but no transferable feeder runtime was reported. Fully resolved 10–30 μm powders remain expensive because stable time step and particle count both worsen | Metal-powder AOR, Hall-type discharge, powder-bed packing, roughness and spreading; Ti-6Al-4V cohesion was inferred by matching simulated and experimental AOR, not from an auger (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000036, pqac-00000037) | **Bulk-test inverse calibration only.** Meier et al. fitted effective surface energy to AOR; this is deterministic calibration rather than Bayesian feeder inversion (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000016) |
| Coupled CFD–DEM | **MFiX-DEM**, LIGGGHTS–OpenFOAM/CFDEM, EDEM–CFD, Fluent–DEM; no strong published precedent was located for a dry, slowly rotating 3 mm micro-auger | DEM contact laws as above plus gas–particle drag, pressure-gradient and possibly lift forces; cohesion can use JKR/SJKR, although coarse-graining must also preserve drag and cohesion similarity | Particle coarse-graining; CFD mesh coarsening; unresolved fluid cells; GPU DEM; reduced stiffness. Simply enlarging particles without consistent coarse-graining can give erroneous, overly rapid filling because air drag changes (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030) | Typically several times more expensive than dry DEM at the same particle count; practical runs range from hours to days. Additional expense is justified when aeration, pneumatic assistance, gas leakage or fine-powder entrainment materially affects flow | In related powder-processing work: filling dynamics, pressure/airflow, suspension velocity and mixing. Direct validation of micro-auger dose increments, no-flow events, taps or afterflow was not identified (pqac-00000030) | **None identified for feeder data.** A future inverse model could infer permeability or effective drag jointly with cohesion, but identifiability would require pressure or airflow observations in addition to balance data |
| Continuum Eulerian granular CFD | Research CFD and commercial solvers such as **OpenFOAM, Fluent or COMSOL**; the cited compression-feed-screw work used a compressible continuum framework (pqac-00000027) | Compressible granular continuum with pressure-dependent density, yield stress and strain-rate dependence; possible frictional-plastic, Drucker–Prager/Mohr–Coulomb or `μ(I)` closures. No particle contact law is resolved | Fixed Eulerian mesh; steady or rotating-reference formulations; reduced-order constitutive laws; much lower degrees of freedom than particle-resolved DEM | Commonly minutes to hours per operating point, depending on mesh and moving-boundary treatment; far cheaper than true-size DEM, but constitutive calibration dominates uncertainty | Pressure, torque, densification, plug formation and mean throughput in compression screws. Evidence for validating milligram-scale increment fluctuations, individual taps, afterflow or zero-flow probability is lacking (pqac-00000027) | **No feeder-based Bayesian property inference identified.** In principle suitable for inferring bulk yield locus, compressibility and wall friction, but not unique particle-scale surface energy or restitution |
| Analytical / reduced-order feed-factor models | Spreadsheet, MATLAB/Python, process simulators and control-system implementations; no DEM code required | Mass flow represented by screw displacement × effective density × speed × fill/volumetric efficiency. Hybrid models add hopper stress, pressure-dependent densification, vortex efficiency and first-order-plus-dead-time dynamics: `ṁ = nPAρ_eη` (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000024) | Intrinsically reduced order; fitted feed-factor curves, response surfaces, Gaussian-process/kriging surrogates and state-space/FOPDT models enable real-time prediction and control | Milliseconds per evaluation; calibration requires experimental sweeps but posterior sampling is inexpensive | Steady and dynamic mass flow, screw-speed response, hopper-level dependence, density drift, refill transients and low-dose precision. Displacement-feed-factor experiments explicitly captured powder densification, dilation and elastic recovery (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000028) | **Best-established route for operational parameter estimation, but generally empirical rather than physics-identifying.** Published models fit gains, delays, effective density and efficiency; they do not uniquely recover cohesion or microscopic friction. They are well suited as emulators or discrepancy models around a smaller DEM training set (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000023) |


*Table: Comparison of particle-resolved, coupled, continuum, and reduced-order approaches for screw-feeder and powder micro-dosing simulations. The table emphasizes codes, physical models, acceleration strategies, validation evidence, computational burden, and whether feeder data have been used for inverse property inference.*

| Rank | Method | Suitability Rating | Strengths for this application | Limitations for this application | Recommended Use Case |
|---:|---|:---:|---|---|---|
| 1 | DEM with Hertz–Mindlin + SJKR/JKR cohesion (**LIGGGHTS**) | ★★★★★ | Resolves particle contacts, force chains, wall friction, rolling resistance, cohesion, outlet bridging, intermittent flow, tapping, and afterflow; directly predicts mass per revolution and zero-flow increments. The existing salt result provides unusually strong application-specific validation. LIGGGHTS supports Hertz–Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, EPSD2 rolling resistance, parallel execution, and coarse-graining (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000029) | True 10–100 µm particles require large particle counts and small time steps; SJKR cohesion-energy density is an effective, model-dependent parameter; coarse-graining can distort arching and outlet intermittency when coarse particles become too large relative to the 3 mm outlet | Primary calibration model. Retain the validated salt configuration, add moisture-conditioned cohesion and wall parameters, and train a surrogate for Bayesian inference from mass/revolution, taps, afterflow, and no-flow statistics |
| 2 | DEM with Hertz–Mindlin + JKR (**EDEM or Rocky**) | ★★★★☆ | JKR surface-energy adhesion is physically interpretable for fine powders; commercial preprocessing, moving geometry, particle-shape tools, and GPU solvers simplify parameter sweeps. EDEM studies have represented cohesive screw and twin-screw transport, mixing, residence time, discharge, and refill (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000007) | License cost and reduced reproducibility; inferred JKR surface energy is not numerically interchangeable with LIGGGHTS SJKR cohesion-energy density. True PSD and nonspherical particles remain expensive, and published validation is mainly for larger feeders or granulators rather than milligram doses | Best commercial cross-check or GPU alternative; useful for testing JKR versus SJKR, particle shape, refill mixing, and whether inferred parameters transfer between solvers |
| 3 | Analytical or reduced-order feed-factor models | ★★★★☆ | Evaluations take milliseconds and are therefore ideal for closed-loop control and Bayesian sampling. Models combine screw displacement, speed, effective density, filling efficiency, hopper stress, densification, and first-order/dead-time dynamics; displacement-feed-factor measurements capture densification and dilation (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000028) | Parameters such as effective density, efficiency, gain, and time constant are lumped quantities; they generally cannot uniquely identify microscopic cohesion, sliding friction, or rolling friction. Bridging, taps, and stochastic no-flow increments require additional state or hurdle models | Real-time digital twin and control model; use as the emulator/discrepancy layer around a limited DEM design, with separate probabilistic models for no-flow events and tap-released mass |
| 4 | Coupled CFD–DEM | ★★★☆☆ | Adds gas pressure, permeability, drag, aeration, and entrainment while retaining particle contacts and cohesion. It may explain speed-dependent fluidization, powder puffing, humidity-conditioned permeability, or delayed settling that dry DEM misses | More expensive and less identifiable than dry DEM; gas coupling is probably secondary at 1–30 rpm unless very fine, low-density, or aerated powders are used. Coarse-graining must preserve both contact and drag similarity; simply enlarging particles can produce incorrect filling dynamics (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030) | Escalation model only when dry DEM leaves systematic residuals correlated with speed, powder permeability, density, outlet pressure, or air displacement; add pressure measurements before inferring drag parameters |
| 5 | Continuum Eulerian granular CFD with Drucker–Prager, Mohr–Coulomb, compressible-plastic, or μ(I) closure | ★★☆☆☆ | Far cheaper than particle-resolved DEM; suitable for mean stress, density, plug formation, torque, pressure, and average throughput. Bulk shear-cell and compressibility data can parameterize yield and densification laws (pqac-00000027) | A 3 mm outlet and 10–100 µm particles provide only tens of particle diameters across the opening; continuum averaging suppresses discrete arches, individual avalanches, tap release, afterflow grains, and zero-dose increments. Constitutive parameters are not direct particle properties | Screening mean throughput, hopper stress, and densification at larger scale; not the primary model for milligram increment statistics or microscopic-property inference |
| 6 | SPH or material point method (MPM) granular continuum | ★☆☆☆☆ | Handles large deformation, free surfaces, contact with moving screws, and elasto-plastic constitutive laws without severe mesh distortion; potentially useful for cohesive plugs | No persuasive published precedent was identified for dry micro-auger dosing. Resolution needed near a 3 mm outlet erodes the expected speed advantage, while stochastic particle-scale stoppages and taps remain unresolved; calibration would require a new constitutive and numerical-validation program | Exploratory research only—consider for strongly compacted, paste-like, or plug-forming material after DEM and conventional continuum models prove inadequate |


*Table: Ranking of simulation approaches for a millimetre-scale auger dispensing cohesive 10–100 µm powders and salts. Particle-resolved cohesive DEM ranks highest, while reduced-order models are the preferred fast companion for inference and control.*

info.query: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. Which physics-based simulation methods have been used to model screw or auger feeders and the micro-dosing of powders: DEM with any contact model, coupled CFD-DEM, continuum approaches (material point method, SPH, FEM with Drucker-Prager or mu(I) rheology), cellular automata, and analytical or reduced-order feed-factor models? For each method give the codes used (open-source such as LIGGGHTS, LAMMPS granular, MercuryDPM, Yade, Project Chrono, MFiX, Blaze-DEM, or commercial such as EDEM, Rocky, PFC), the contact and cohesion models, speed-ups (coarse-graining, reduced Young's modulus, GPU), typical computational cost, what was validated against experiments (mass flow rate, feed factor, fluctuations, refill), and which studies used the simulation to infer powder properties from feeder data. Rank the methods by suitability for a millimetre-scale auger dosing cohesive fine powders (10-100 micrometres) and salts, and list concrete published input parameters we could reuse.
